This formulation not only preserves the edge-attributed multigraph structure of transaction networks but also reduces every aggregation step to plaintext--ciphertext matrix products. Since CKKS can evaluate only polynomial circuits, we also approximate each nonlinearity with a composite polynomial of the sign function, which we calibrate per activation site. On the IBM AML benchmark, our model achieves performance competitive with plaintext baselines, and with a consumer-grade GPU, classifies each queried transaction end-to-end in as little as \textbf{5.31} seconds, while per-transaction latency can be amortized to \textbf{1.65} seconds when optimized for throughput.

Machine Learning.title: LADDER: A Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation Benchmark
Machine Learning.summary: General-purpose robot manipulation policies learn short-horizon skills effectively, but degrade rapidly on long-horizon tasks. Existing benchmarks cannot isolate failures because task horizon is either too short or entangled with scene and object variations. We propose LADDER, a long-horizon robot manipulation benchmark scaling from 1 to 10 subgoals within the same environment over three suites (SimplerEnv-Long, RobotArena-$\infty$-Long, and RoboLab-Long), 145 tasks, eight categories, two embodiments, and 2,024 simulated episodes per system. We evaluate two orchestration paradigms: text subgoals for learned low-level policies (VoLo) and tool selection orchestration (CaP-X, GPT-Policy, PSP-Agent, TiPToP). Given the full instruction directly, low-level policies achieve 85.4% on single-subgoal tasks, but drop to near zero on extended tasks. While orchestration remedies this, it remains bounded by physical execution errors of the low-level policy rather than high-level planning and achieves only ~25%. Tool selection orchestration with GPT-Policy on GPT-6 Astra significantly outperforms learned-policy methods, but incurs significant time and cost budget and succeeds only ~62%. Real-world experiments across two embodiments confirm the collapse of the low-level policy and the gain from orchestration. Project website: https://ladder.insait.ai

Machine Learning.title: inLoRA-MINT: Internal Representations for Auditing Training Data in Domain-adapted LLMs
Machine Learning.summary:
This work investigates the application of the Membership Inference Test (MINT) to large language models (LLMs) fine-tuned with LoRA, aiming to determine whether specific samples were used during training and address concerns about data privacy, leakage, and transparency. Building on our previous LoRA-MINT framework, which relies exclusively on perplexity under a strict black-box setting, we propose an approach based on intermediate model representations, including activations and parameter-dependent signals. These representations enable a MINT classifier to distinguish training from non-training samples without requiring full access to model parameters.
  We evaluated the method on four LLMs (Qwen, Phi-4, DeepSeek-V3, and LLaMA 3.2-3B) fine-tuned on three datasets covering medical, mathematical, and academic reasoning tasks. Results show consistent performance across architectures and domains, achieving scores between 95% and 98%, with robustness to variations in model configurations and data distributions. The proposed approach enables efficient auditing of sensitive training data and supports data provenance and compliance with emerging privacy and AI governance regulations. Although our experiments focus on LoRA-based fine-tuning, the methodology can be extended to other LLM adaptation techniques and, more broadly, to other AI models.

Machine Learning.title: Forecasting Brain Tracer Distribution from Pre-Contrast MRI: A Comparison of Direct Regression and Flow Matching
Machine Learning.summary: Intrathecal contrast-enhanced MRI shows how a tracer injected into the cerebrospinal fluid spreads through the brain, but requires repeated scans over 24--48\,h. We therefore ask how much of the later tracer distribution can be predicted from the pre-contrast scan and elapsed time alone. Using 104 training patients (878 MRI volumes), we compared a direct image-to-image regression model with a more complex generative model based on conditional flow matching, and tested both on 23 held-out patients and on 51 patients from a separate cohort with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (INPH). The direct model reduced the error of simply copying the pre-contrast scan by about 60\% in held-out patients and 25\% in the INPH cohort, and its predicted change maps agreed with the observed tracer enhancement rather than only reproducing anatomy. The generative model was less accurate in both cohorts. A substantial part of the later tracer distribution is therefore predictable from the patient's brain anatomy as seen on pre-contrast MRI, and the added model complexity gave no benefit at this data scale. With prospective validation, such forecasts could be studied for patient stratification and treatment planning in intrathecal therapies.

Machine Learning.title: High-fidelity Three-Dimensional Flow Field Reconstruction Driven by Turbulent Fluid Dynamics
Machine Learning.summary: High-fidelity three-dimensional turbulent flow fields are essential for scientific and engineering analyses, yet obtaining them through direct numerical simulation or high-resolution measurements remains expensive. Super-resolution reconstruction from coarse-grained data therefore offers a promising alternative, but remains fundamentally challenging because fine-scale structures are intrinsically three-dimensional and dynamically coupled across scales. Existing data-driven approaches still struggle to recover multiscale volumetric structures and their coherent temporal evolution. To address these limitations, we propose a turbulence-aware framework for time-resolved three-dimensional flow reconstruction. The framework couples a multiscale neural operator, designed to recover volumetric structures, with a state space model to promote temporal consistency in the reconstructed dynamics. In addition, Navier-Stokes residuals are incorporated as soft constraints to regularize the reconstruction toward physically plausible dynamics. A mixture-of-experts mechanism is also introduced to support unsupervised adaptation to unknown coarse-graining. Across evaluations on canonical turbulent systems and atmospheric reanalysis data, the proposed framework reduces reconstruction errors relative to learning-based and classical baselines, while better preserving multiscale spatial structure and coherent temporal evolution. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in reconstructing high-fidelity three-dimensional flow fields from coarse-grained data.
Machine Learning.comment: 66 pages, 9 main-text figures and 1 main-text table; includes Supplementary Information with 14 figures and 22 tables

Machine Learning.title: Cover meets Robbins while Betting on Bounded Data: $\ln n$ Regret and Almost Sure $\ln\ln n$ Regret
Machine Learning.summary: Consider betting against a sequence of $[0,1]$-valued observations using bets that are fair if the data have a conditional mean $m_0 \in (0,1)$. Cover's universal portfolio algorithm achieves a worst-case regret of $O(\ln n)$ compared to the best constant bet in hindsight, and this logarithmic order is unimprovable against adversarial data. We construct an explicit full-support Robbins mixture that combines insights from Robbins and Cover. It retains $O(\ln n)$ regret on every path while also eventually satisfying $R_n\le(1+o(1))\ln\ln V_n$ on every path with bounded mixture wealth and $V_n\to\infty$, where $V_n$ is an intrinsic variance process. It also attains the optimal asymptotic wealth growth rate under iid alternatives. Under the conditional-mean claim and almost-sure divergence of $V_n$, the sharper regret bound holds almost surely, and its leading constant $1$ is unimprovable. We also give explicit finite-time, path-wise regret bounds. A simple hedging principle shows how splitting initial wealth between two strategies achieves a best-of-both-worlds guarantee by retaining the smaller of their regrets and the larger of their growth rates. We contrast our results to those for unbounded data in Agrawal and Ramdas (2026). Their worst-case regret is unbounded. However, hedging yields almost-sure iterated-logarithmic regret together with optimal growth. Finally, our wealth process witnesses a sharp game-theoretic upper law of iterated logarithm, analogous to Shafer and Vovk (2005).

Machine Learning.title: Weighting-Based Strategies for Classification: Analysis and Local Peak Dynamics with CART Trees
Machine Learning.summary: Tabular learning tasks often suffer from class imbalance, which is often addressed via weighting-based strategies. In this work, we compare the naive approach (unweighted) with the weighting-based rebalancing strategies. Somewhat surprisingly, we demonstrate that, asymptotically, as the predictor complexity increases with sample size, weighting strategies yield predictive performance identical to unweighted approaches across all evaluation metrics, up to a shift in the final threshold. To go beyond, we theoretically study the estimation of a linear regression function through weighted and unweighted CART trees with limited depths. In this setting, we prove that the points in the PR space for both strategies are distributed along the same curve, thus illustrating the similar nonasymptotic performance of the two strategies. Then, we numerically identify more complex synthetic settings where performance gaps, evaluated via fixed classifier complexity, favor weighting strategies. Thus, to guide practitioners, we introduce an indicator that aims at signaling whether a data set may benefit from weighting.

Machine Learning.title: PICPIs: Prediction-Interval-Conditional Prediction Intervals
Machine Learning.summary: A classical question in statistics is which observable quantities to condition on when drawing inferences about unobservable targets. For conformal prediction in nonparametric uncertainty quantification, standard marginal validity offers limited resolution at the prediction values on which decisions are based, and fully conditional guarantees with respect to the covariates are provably unattainable. We address this gap by introducing a prediction-based conditioning framework that we refer to as Prediction-Interval-Conditional Prediction Intervals (PICPIs). Formally, a PICPI is an interval $I$ satisfying a self-consistency condition: $$\mathbb{E} [Y \mid p(X) \in I] \in I,$$ for predictive model $p$, contextual covariate $X$, and outcome $Y$. Thus, an interval simultaneously defines a stratum of prediction values and certifies that the mean outcome in that stratum lies in the same interval. This self-consistency condition yields data-adaptive strata without altering the original prediction. Such intervals can be constructed using practical algorithms. Under regularity of the prediction distribution, the constructed intervals cover all but an arbitrarily small fraction of prediction values and have widths that decrease at rate $n^{-1/3}$, up to logarithmic factors and the prediction error. Moreover, identifying these locally calibrated intervals can, in turn, inform downstream decision-making. We derive inference procedures for PICPIs in probabilistic prediction and multi-class classification, accompanied by theoretical guarantees. Empirical results are provided that compare PICPIs with existing interval-based baselines.

Machine Learning.title: Can Machine Learning Potentials Be More Accurate Than the Methods They Are Trained On?
Machine Learning.summary: Although machine learning potentials (MLPs) generalize across configurational and chemical compound spaces, their accuracy is commonly believed to be limited by their training methods, with improvements beyond this limit achieved so far only by refitting to experimental observables. In this Perspective, we argue that MLPs can also be made more accurate than their training methods non-empirically by generalizing across a third space, that of quantum-chemical methods. We propose routes to method-transferable MLPs that predict at unseen methods, with working implementations in both density-functional and wavefunction-based theories showing that they can be more accurate than any of their training methods. Aiming beyond the accuracy of the training methods could also make universal MLPs more accurate than single-method models, even when the method-transferable MLPs remain less accurate than those QM methods. Method-transferable MLPs will shape the construction of training datasets and the evaluation of models, pushing the accuracy limits of chemical simulations.

Machine Learning.title: ChampionKV: Head-Wise Adaptive Budget Allocation for KV Cache Compression
Machine Learning.summary: Some observation-window-based KV cache compressors use prompt attention to identify important tokens but allocate uniform or predefined budgets across heads, overlooking input-dependent differences in budget demand. We propose ChampionKV, an input-adaptive head-wise budget allocator for long-context KV cache compression. It uses the maximum aggregated observation-window attention score as a lightweight empirical proxy for attention concentration, assigning larger budgets to heads with dispersed attention and smaller budgets to concentrated heads. An abnormal-head mask and a floor-budget mechanism improve robustness under weak attention responses. ChampionKV plugs into compressors such as SnapKV and PyramidKV without changing their token-selection procedures. On LongBench and RULER, both Champion variants consistently improve over their SnapKV and PyramidKV base compressors; the improvements are largest and statistically significant on Llama3.1-70B-Instruct, especially under tight budgets, whereas results on the tested 7B/8B models remain competitive but mixed. ChampionKV does not uniformly outperform Ada-KV, whose global cross-head Top-K selection retains an advantage in several settings. Controlled analysis further shows improved retained attention mass over the corresponding base compressors at negligible overhead.

Machine Learning.title: SHELDON: Reasoning through Dual Search over Hypothesis and Observation Spaces
Machine Learning.summary: Test-time scaling has enabled LLMs to solve increasingly complex reasoning, discovery, and optimization tasks. However, existing approaches often gather observations while seeking evidence for current hypotheses, then generate new hypotheses conditioned on those hypotheses and their associated evidence. This couples observation discovery to existing hypotheses, favoring local refinements over exploration of unknown hypotheses regions. Inspired by the hypothetico-deductive method (Hempel, 1945) and dual-space models of scientific discovery (Klahr & Dunbar, 1988), we introduce SHELDON, a scientific reasoning harness that separately represents and jointly explores hypothesis and observation spaces. By actively seeking new observations along with new hypotheses, SHELDON can discover observations that its current hypotheses do not explain. These unexplained observations expose gaps in its understanding, motivate new investigations, and guide the generation of hypotheses beyond refinements of existing ones. Across diagnosis, abstract reasoning, and optimization benchmarks, SHELDON outperforms evaluated baselines by up to 26.7 points. Additional analysis shows that SHELDON generates up to 4.5x more novel solutions.

Machine Learning.title: FRACTION: Fraud Explanation Generation via Agentic Graph Context Navigation
Machine Learning.summary: Graph fraud explanation generation emerges as an important task, which requires jointly leveraging graph structure and content information to produce human-readable explanations for a given risk label. An intuitive approach is to adapt existing graph-enhanced large language models (LLMs), which inject graph structure into LLMs via graph-conditioned instruction tuning or structure-aware embeddings. However, existing methods face two key challenges in graph fraud explanation generation: a lack of evaluation protocols tailored to explanation quality, and a mismatch between the granularity of graph information they provide and what explanation generation requires. In this paper, we propose FRaud Explanation Generation via Agentic Graph Context NavigaTION (FRACTION), a framework for graph fraud explanation generation. To evaluate explanation quality, we introduce a task-specific rubric that assesses faithfulness, graph grounding, helpfulness, consistency, and conciseness, and validate it against human judgments. To focus on fine-grained details of relevant neighbors without reading the entire neighborhood, we equip a language model with graph tools that progressively disclose neighbor records. To train our graph agent, we propose a rubric-guided trajectory distillation strategy through which the agent learns both tool-use behavior and structured explanation generation. Experimental results on three fraud datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines under a human-aligned rubric.

Machine Learning.title: The Geography of Algorithmic Judgment: LLM Intermediaries, Place Identity, and Racial Steering in Housing Search
Machine Learning.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly assuming an intermediary role in housing search through the integration of listing platforms within conversational interfaces, mediating access to information, search, and recommendations within urban settings. We expand on prior work on racial steering in LLMs by conducting a behavioral audit of seven open-weight and closed-source LLMs across four U.S. cities, testing location recommendations across three iterative prompting conditions that progressively add lifestyle preference context and reflect fair housing paired-testing methodologies. We find that steering is an emergent behavior of the model's interpretive license rather than primarily a static property. Steering results from the interaction of a user's identity, preference articulation, and the spatial logic that a model has internalized about learned representations of place, preference, and opportunity in a given city, and how different types of users relate to it. While steering was present, it was not uniform in direction or magnitude across evaluated conditions. Preference-conditioned testing often increased or reconfigured the number of models that exhibited steering behaviors relative to baseline conditions, suggesting that LLMs may interpret what the same housing preference means differently depending on the racial identity of the user. Our findings also demonstrate that the city is not a neutral testing unit for LLM evaluation in place-based sectors, and results from one local market cannot be assumed to generalize to another. Local and domain expertise will be required in the housing sector to ensure that legal and institutional commitments to fair housing are not undermined while adopting AI tools that mediate spatial access.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at AIES '26. 14 pages with supplemental tables and figures in complement to the main conference paper

Machine Learning.title: Correcting or Continuing? What On-Policy Distillation Learns from Student Errors
Machine Learning.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher, mitigating the distribution mismatch of off-policy supervision. While prior work has primarily trained on problems a student can largely solve, we ask whether OPD can improve a student when training is restricted to problems it currently fails. We evaluate five representative OPD mechanisms with Qwen-3 and Phi-4 models under a unified competition-mathematics protocol. We find that OPD does not improve accuracy on this hard subset, with most mechanisms instead degrading performance despite continued decreases in training KL divergence. All eight configurations show a decline, and the two-sided sign test gives p=0.0078. In contrast, the same pipeline improves accuracy by 4.6 percentage points when training is not concentrated on failures, showing that the failure is conditional on the training regime rather than systematic. These findings suggest that OPD is effective when supervision is dominated by correct student prefixes, but can reinforce existing errors when training is concentrated on problems the student currently fails.

Machine Learning.title: Bayesian Nonparametric Thompson Sampling for Multi-Armed Bandits
Machine Learning.summary:
In stochastic multi-armed bandits, rewards are generated by an unknown distribution; the world's reward uncertainty induces the exploration-exploitation trade-off. Thompson sampling (TS) addresses this trade-off elegantly, but requires knowing the reward model's parametric form to sample from its posterior and compute per-arm expected rewards ---which limits its applicability as it demands per-scenario model specification and hyperparameter tuning.
  We here adopt Bayesian nonparametric (BNP) mixture models to remove this requirement, extending TS to arbitrary reward distributions. We model each arm's unknown reward distribution with an independent BNP Gaussian mixture, which can approximate any continuous reward density, and adapts its complexity to sequentially observed data. Embedding the BNP mixture model into TS yields Nonparametric TS, an algorithm that sequentially learns the reward model that best approximates the true, yet unknown, per-arm reward distribution, avoiding case-by-case model specification and hyperparameter tuning.
  We empirically demonstrate that ($i$) Nonparametric TS matches the regret performance of Oracle TS policies that know the true reward model; ($ii$) it favorably compares (in cumulative regret and volatility) to a suite of state-of-the-art alternatives across multimodal, outlier-contaminated, and non-exponential-family reward distributions; and ($iii$) its Bayesian nonparametric inference remains computationally practical and accurate for regret minimization.
Machine Learning.comment: The software used for this study is publicly available at https://github.com/iurteaga/bandits

Machine Learning.title: Match the Canvas, Not Just the Answer: Predictability-Aware SFT for Diffusion Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable flexible parallel generation by resolving tokens according to the model's evolving predictability rather than a fixed left-to-right order. This flexibility, however, introduces training choices absent from standard autoregressive teacher forcing: which reference tokens are visible when a target is supervised and how much generation space is allocated. Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically makes these choices through random masking, independently of inference. Our analysis shows how this training-inference mismatch can misdirect supervision. Random masking can conceal prediction errors or penalize uncertainty that decoding would otherwise resolve, while the attention-visible input length can change which response formulations the model favors, even when the underlying solution is unchanged. Motivated by these findings, we propose Predictability-Aware Canvas Selection and Supervision (PACS), an SFT method. PACS uses the model's own predictability to select each example's attention-visible input length and supervises reference tokens immediately before their confidence-guided revelation. Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, PACS consistently achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared SFT methods, with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks. Code will be released upon publication.

Machine Learning.title: ULTRADISCOVERY: Abductive Exploration in an Interconnected, Epistemically Open Universe
Machine Learning.summary: Scientific discovery often begins when scattered clues call for a new way of describing the world. Such abductive exploration can require constructing the representation in which an explanation is stated, when the world is epistemically open, and composing evidence scattered across contexts, when it is structurally interconnected. Existing benchmarks rarely separate these two demands or control them independently. We introduce ULTRADISCOVERY, an interactive world of five domains in which an agent revises an initially successful theory and predicts the outcome of an unseen cross-domain intervention. A $2 \times 2$ design leaves the representation open or discloses it, and leaves the evidence distributed or aligns it, with the latent dynamics fixed. With the representation open, agents across eleven models often retract the axiom they were taught, and none introduces the unobserved entity or rewrites the variables that a replacement requires. Disclosure triples intervention requests and adds about one of the eighteen findings the world affords, and alignment adds less. Two vendor-harness systems carry discovery into more domains, and one of them rewrites the variables in Open episodes. No system makes the exact prediction within 200 paid actions. At larger budgets one exact prediction appears with both aids, while every Open episode remains inexact. The results locate the difficulty in the step from accumulating evidence to composing it into a representation that transfers.

Machine Learning.title: Automatic Thematic Indexing of Large Literary Corpora: A Machine Learning Approach to Voltaire's Complete Works
Machine Learning.summary: Thematic indexing -- the practice of assigning structured conceptual labels to sections of text -- is essential to scholarly access in large-scale literary and historical editions, yet it remains a largely manual, labour-intensive process. This paper explores the application of machine learning to automatic thematic indexing, using two substantial sub-corpora of the Complete Works of Voltaire as a test case: the Essai sur les mœurs et l'esprit des nations and the Questions sur l'Encyclopédie. The task is framed as a multi-label classification problem, in which a model must assign the set of index entries that a professional indexer would apply to a given page of text. We compare a range of approaches -- from encoder-based models with classification heads to generative large language models (LLMs) fine-tuned via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) -- spanning model sizes from approximately 3 to 120 billion parameters. Our best-performing model, from the Mistral family in a 4-bit quantised configuration, achieves F1 scores of up to 0.67; we argue that these figures represent lower bounds, given the inherent subjectivity of professional indexing and the frequency with which model predictions prove semantically valid despite diverging from the print index. We further evaluate cross-corpus generalisation and conduct a detailed qualitative analysis of model behaviour on literary and rhetorical features of the source texts that prove particularly resistant to automated treatment. Our findings have implications for the broader challenge of providing structured thematic access to large-scale literary and historical corpora.

Machine Learning.title: Saliency-Guided Replay for Continual Learning in Deep Spiking Neural Networks
Machine Learning.summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are promising for energy-efficient neuromorphic computing, but they still suffer from catastrophic forgetting when learning tasks sequentially. This work investigates the integration of Experience Packing and Replay (EPR) as a memory-efficient continual learning strategy for deep SNNs under low-latency constraints. The proposed framework combines Batch Normalization Through Time stabilized VGG9 SNNs with Spike Activation Maps (SAM), which provide forward-only explanations based on spike activity. These explanations are temporally aggregated into spatial attention maps and used to select the most informative image patches for replay, instead of storing full images. Experiments on Split CIFAR10 and Split CIFAR100 show that SAM-guided EPR improves the accuracy-memory trade-off under tight memory budgets, and remains competitive while requiring substantially less storage.
Machine Learning.comment: Streaming Continual Learning Workshop. In post-proceeding of International Workshops of ECML PKDD 2026

Machine Learning.title: Convergence rates for generative drifting flows: fixed-scale obstructions and multihead acceleration
Machine Learning.summary: Drifting models offer a promising route to faster generative AI: they perform gradual transport during training, while generating new samples in a single step. This paper asks whether the underlying drifting process can converge rapidly to a target distribution under ideal conditions, before finite-data or optimization effects are introduced. We show that its convergence rate depends critically on how it handles spatial scale. With a single fixed resolution, fine-scale features of the target can become nearly invisible, leading to extremely slow convergence. We introduce a multihead approach that combines scale-normalized information across a continuum of resolutions. We prove that this multihead approach restores exponential convergence near standard reference distributions. These results identify fixed resolution as a key bottleneck and provide a simple route to faster one-step generative models.

Machine Learning.title: Improving Neural Symbolic Regression with a Diverse Prior and Post-training Alignment
Machine Learning.summary: Symbolic regression is the problem of finding an expression that fits a dataset. Solving it requires searching a combinatorial space of candidate expressions. Neural symbolic regression can amortize that search by training a model once on synthetic data and then predicting expressions for a new dataset. But existing models still underperform genetic programming on real, noisy data. We argue that the deficit lies in the training rather than in the paradigm, and present RASR (Reinforced Amortized Symbolic Regression), a method with two key changes to the training recipe. First, we design a synthetic prior that narrows the gap with real-world data: inputs come from the prior of a tabular foundation model; constants are sampled bottom-up, conditioned on the data; targets carry heteroscedastic and structured noise; and everything is standardized. Second, we split training into two stages. Supervised pre-training maximizes the token-level likelihood of a reference expression. This is followed by reinforcement-learning post-training that aligns the model with its inference-time use by rewarding held-out fit and penalizing expression size. On the black-box track of SRBench 2.0, RASR achieves the best mean test $R^2$ rank of all evaluated methods. Three RASR variants, trained with different size penalties, make up most of the accuracy-complexity Pareto front. On Strogatz, our method recovers more ground-truth expressions than any baseline, and on Feynman it is competitive with the best-performing methods.

Machine Learning.title: Counterfactual Certification for Sequential Unlearning with Long-Run Performance Guarantees
Machine Learning.summary: Certified machine unlearning ensures the proximity between the unlearned model and a model retrained without the data to be forgotten. Extending this framework to sequential deletion requests, typically arriving as groups of variable size (e.g., all records of one user or of coordinated users), is challenging. For unlearning methods based on fine-tuning on the retain sets, this leads to either degrading performance or increasing computation as the number of unlearning requests grows. For independent successive requests, we instead certify each model release against a counterfactual unlearning trajectory in which the group being deleted never took part. With a fixed fine-tuning budget per deletion, we show that, for smooth strongly convex objectives, this approach keeps the performance loss bounded, uniformly in the number of requests. Experiments with multiclass logistic regression on FEMNIST show that the resulting algorithm needs fewer corrective steps than existing sequential methods and outperforms training-time differential privacy, particularly when group sizes are heterogeneous.

Machine Learning.title: Exact power indices for plurality-voting ensembles
Machine Learning.summary: Plurality-voting ensembles aggregate the predictions of multiple base classifiers and output the most voted class, with ties typically broken at random. Despite the simple aggregation rule, attributing the impact of each base classifier to the ensemble's predictions is far from straightforward. That is, a single base classifier's impact depends on how it interacts with the votes of all other classifiers in the ensemble, for example, in resolving ties, and not only on its own predictions. We address the attribution problem using established tools from cooperative game theory, studying the Banzhaf and Shapley power indices for new games modeling plurality voting and random tie-breaking, for binary and multiclass classification settings. Computing power indices is, in general, intractable. Surprisingly, our methods, collectively named ENPOWER, enable the exact computation of Banzhaf and Shapley values in linear time for the binary classification setting and in low-degree polynomial time for the multiclass setting. The algorithms in ENPOWER rely on new combinatorial formulations of the Banzhaf and Shapley indices, yielding closed-form solutions for the binary case and ordinary generating function representations for the multiclass case. We validate empirically the methods in ENPOWER demonstrating their high applicability, providing attribution values not captured by existing methods. We apply the attribution of ENPOWER to: ensemble pruning and prompt-based ensembling of vision-language models.
Machine Learning.comment: Extended version of a work accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 59 pages, 9 figures, 11 tables

Machine Learning.title: All-electron machine-learned orbital-free density functional for periodic CHNO systems
Machine Learning.summary: We introduce STRUCTURES-P, a machine-learned all-electron orbital-free density functional for periodic CHNO systems. Electrostatics are evaluated analytically in an atom-centered Gaussian basis, while an equivariant network learns the kinetic and exchange-correlation energy from energies and gradients of non-ground-state densities. Minimizing the functional from a superposition of atomic densities recovers the Kohn-Sham ground state: on held-out crystals, the density error falls from 6.7% to 0.4% of the electron count and the energy error reaches 0.25 mHa per atom, half that of a same-architecture interatomic potential. A single functional can be trained for both isolated molecules and periodic systems, and the model generalizes to larger unit cells. It largely preserves relative-energy rankings and reproduces convex-hull vertices on the tested H-N composition slice. Together, these results demonstrate the viability of machine-learned all-electron orbital-free DFT for variational density optimization and energy evaluation in fixed-geometry solids.
Machine Learning.comment: 37 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables (including Supplementary Information). Supplementary Data 1 will be available with the journal version

Machine Learning.title: Rarity Determines Minimax Rates of Semantic Entropy From Weak Pairwise Judgments With a Known Channel
Machine Learning.summary: The semantic entropy of a language model is the entropy of the meanings of its sampled answers. The meanings are never observed, and the entropy is estimated from the verdicts of a pairwise equivalence judge. Given the meanings of $n$ answers, a known channel declares each pair equivalent independently, with probability $q+Δ$ within a meaning and $q$ across meanings. At most $K$ meanings occur, and $q$ is bounded away from $0$ and $1$. For a weak judge, with $nΔ^2\to0$, the global minimax rate is set by distributions near a vertex of the simplex and overstates the difficulty elsewhere. We show that the difficulty is set by how many meanings can be rare. Over distributions with at most $s$ meanings below a fixed probability $τ<1/(K-s)$, the minimax squared risk is of order $N^{-1/s}$ for $s\ge2$, $N^{-1}\log^2(e+N)$ for $s=1$ and $N^{-1}$ for $s=0$, capped at one, where $N=n^KΔ^{2K-2}$. The matching lower bounds hold on every fixed polynomial window $nΔ^2\le n^{-κ}$. One estimator attains these rates without knowing $s$ or $τ$: it averages products of centered verdicts along all spanning trees of every $k$-set of answers, projects the resulting power sums onto the valid moment set and inverts them. The case $s=K-1$ gives the global rate $N^{-1/(K-1)}$ and the consistency threshold: with $Δ=n^{-γ}$ the entropy is uniformly consistently estimable exactly when $γ<K/(2K-2)$. On polynomial windows, the same estimator attains the sharp local minimax constant on shrinking neighborhoods of interior points with distinct probabilities. Restricting the average to stars multiplies the constant by $K^{K-3}$.

Machine Learning.title: AlignPred: Error-Controlled KV Cache Compression via Alignment and Predictive Coding
Machine Learning.summary: Long-running agents retain KV caches across turns and sessions for hours or days. Compressing these persistent caches requires reducing storage while controlling reconstruction error. We present AlignPred, a codec that combines local alignment with predictive coding under a configurable KV reconstruction-error budget. Local orthogonal transforms align related heads or layers into a common coordinate frame, allowing AlignPred to combine token-wise prediction with same-token prediction across heads or layers. Residuals are quantized on an error-bounded lattice and entropy-coded, without learned predictors, encoder-side mode search, or large joint transforms. Across three attention mechanisms, AlignPred requires less storage than the evaluated baselines at comparable measured reconstruction error. Against the evaluated CPU codec implementations, it decodes at least 1.6 times faster while matching or improving encode time. AlignPred achieves near-native task scores at substantially compressed operating points on LongBench-Pro at 128K context. AlignPred's SGLang HiCache integration reduces persistent target-KV storage by 42-72% relative to native HiCache, with comparable latency.

Machine Learning.title: Neural Dimensional Analysis: Foundations of Dimensionless and Scale-Consistent Computation
Machine Learning.summary: Modern Transformers rely on many scale-control mechanisms, including normalization, residual scaling, attention temperatures, loss weighting, and adaptive updates. To explain how these mechanisms maintain scale consistency, we introduce Neural Dimensional Analysis (NDA), a unified framework based on dimensional consistency. We define neural units that specify how tensors rescale and which quantities can be added, just as physical units do in physics. Our rules match residual units, nondimensionalize attention and gate inputs, combine losses across units, and convert gradient units into parameter units. We implement NDA through dimensionless Unit Violation Indices (UVI) for diagnosing scale mismatches within Transformers, a unit-consistent multi-loss objective, and the Gauge-Canonical Transformer (GCT) with normalized coordinates and orthogonalized residual additions. In language-model experiments spanning 51M to 1B parameters, GCT remains stable during training across a broad sixteenfold learning-rate range, outperforming Pre-LN, LLaMA-style, and QK-Norm in 124M validation loss at tuned learning rates. GCT's normalized residual stream also shows improved robustness to quantization. At 1B parameters, calibrated per-tensor int8 quantization increases GCT's validation loss by only 0.009 nats, compared with up to 5.51 nats for the baselines. Vision and physics-informed neural network experiments further confirm NDA's benefits beyond language modeling. These results establish dimensional consistency as a neural network design principle.

Machine Learning.title: Probe and Skip: Self-Predictive Token Skipping for Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference
Machine Learning.summary: Long-context inference enhances the reasoning capability of Large Language Models (LLMs), but incurs significant computational overhead. Token-oriented methods, such as pruning and skipping, have shown great promise in reducing inference latency, yet still suffer from inherently insufficient structure optimization, outdated selection criteria, and redundancy interference, resulting in suboptimal speed-accuracy trade-off. To address these issues, we propose a novel training-free framework dubbed Self-Predictive Token Skipping (SPTS), for efficient long-context LLM inference. Specifically, motivated by probing the influence of target layers prior to skipping, we design two selective token skipping strategies for typical structures, including Partial Attention Probing (PAP) for multi-head attention and Low-rank Transformation Probing (LTP) for feed forward network. The former selects informative tokens via partial forward attention computation, while the latter constructs a low-rank proxy network to predict token transformations. In addition, a Multi-Stage Delayed Pruning (MSDP) strategy reallocates skipping budgets and progressively removes redundant tokens across layers. Extensive experiments display the effectiveness of our method, achieving up to 2.46$\times$ and 2.29$\times$ speedups for prefilling and end-to-end generation, respectively, while maintaining state-of-the-art accuracy. The source code is available at https://github.com/Wuzimeng/SPTS.

Machine Learning.title: BELT : BEhavior-Aligned Low-Rank KV Cache Compression with Learned Top-k Rank Allocation
Machine Learning.summary: Long-context inference makes the key-value (KV) cache a major memory bottleneck for large language models. We propose BELT, a low-rank KV cache compression framework. Its key-side objective targets attention distributions rather than raw keys or pre-softmax logits, yielding a quadratic surrogate with a closed-form low-rank solution. A learned global rank allocator uses differentiable soft selection during training and hard selection at deployment to meet a user-specified component budget. Experiments demonstrate improved model quality under aggressive compression and increased decoding throughput at comparable accuracy. Evaluated across three LLMs and multiple benchmarks, BELT achieves up to 70% low-rank KV cache compression while outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 23.3 points on LongBench, and up to 17.8x overall KV cache reduction when combined with quantization. With Triton-based GPU kernels and a quantized cache, BELT delivers up to 2.7x speedup for the attention module and 3.3x end-to-end decoding throughput.

Machine Learning.title: Better Capturing Interactions Between Products in~Retail: Revisited Negative Sampling for~Basket Choice Modeling
Machine Learning.summary: Brick-and-mortar retailers face many different challenges that involve understanding thoroughly its products catalog and customer preferences. In particular, assortment optimization - proposing the ideal mix of products - and promotion planning hold a pivotal role in their strategy. By leveraging sales data, retailers can make informed decisions on which products to sell and how to manage inventory, based on customer preferences as well as regional and seasonal trends. It is especially crucial to capture interactions between products, in order to minimize the number of items that cannibalize each other's sales and to ensure that complementary products, which are often purchased together, are conjointly available and sold across all stores. In this paper, we propose a model of shopping basket that learns embeddings to represent interactions between products, prices and stores. Our model is built to uncover sales patterns from very large transaction datasets. In particular, the optimization loss is computed with random negative samples in order to overcome the computational bottlenecks that arise with large number of items. Our experiments on synthetic data show the efficiency of drawing such negative samples based on the actual assortment of available products, with better results than approaches from the literature. We also validate our approach by training and evaluating our model on a dataset composed of millions of transactions from Fortenova Group, one of the leading retail company in Southeast Europe. Our model showcases promising applications in the sector of retail, with enriched interfaces to efficiently support category managers.

Machine Learning.title: CALM-5G: Event-Level Conformal Risk Control for Predictive Service-Assurance Alarms
Machine Learning.summary: Predictive service assurance converts forecasts of key performance indicators into alarms, and that conversion decides whether the assurance function is deployable. We present CALM-5G, an assurance layer that operates above any forecasting backbone and issues alarms with distribution-free, finite-sample guarantees. It calibrates on service-level violation events, scores violation onset directly, selects its calibration scheme out of sample, and reports the alarm duty cycle with every certified miss rate. Four corpora are evaluated separately, namely a production cellular network, commercial 5G traces, an open radio access network testbed and our 5G standalone testbed. Risk control on the regression-derived score yields duty cycles of 0.24 to 0.91. Onset targeting with cross-validated calibration reduces time-in-alarm by 56.3% to 89.7% on three corpora, with no significant change on the fourth. The realised miss rate stays within a two-standard-error tolerance on three corpora and within one standard error of it on the fourth. Under label shift, pooled batch calibration exceeds that tolerance structurally, by 10.9 standard errors on the production corpus. Online calibration restores compliance. Calibration schemes cannot be ranked on the split that fits their thresholds. Miss rate and duty cycle are certified jointly where within-entity dependence leaves sufficient calibration units.
Machine Learning.comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Network and Service Management

Machine Learning.title: Learning Distributions from Samples and Qualities
Machine Learning.summary: We study parameter estimation when each sample from a continuous parametric distribution is accompanied by a binary quality label governed by the same unknown parameter. By imposing hard feasibility constraints, deterministic labels can accelerate estimation from the classical $n^{-1/2}$ rate of smooth quality-aware M-estimators to $n^{-1}$. Combining PAC guarantees with local error-to-parameter conversions, we establish this rate for both identifiable and finitely ambiguous quality classifiers, with likelihood information resolving the latter ambiguity. When the quality model is known only up to an additive constant, we construct threshold-free pairwise preferences from oppositely labeled samples and retain the accelerated rate despite the unknown threshold. We further show that pointwise qualities and pairwise preferences are incomparable: either can be strictly more informative than the other. Our assumptions hold for Gaussian, Laplace, and exponential families under thresholded log-likelihood rewards. Finally, a minimax lower bound establishes the optimal $n^{-1}$ dependence on sample size, up to logarithmic and dimension-dependent factors, while experiments confirm the benefits of constraint-based estimation.

Machine Learning.title: HaloBlock: Faster and Better Decoding for Diffusion Large Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have attracted increasing research attention due to their bidirectional attention and arbitrary order decoding. However, there are two issues in dLLMs inference: the decoding difficulty is dominated by the tokens on the right side of the block, and the block-wise decoding inherently suffers from boundary contextual discontinuity. To tackle these limitations, we propose HaloBlock, a difficulty-aware adaptive halo mechanism for dLLM inference. We first leverage bidirectional cumulative entropy to characterize block decoding difficulty. Then, based on the bidirectional decoding difficulty, we adaptively allocate bidirectional halo regions on both sides of each block to mitigate boundary contextual discontinuity. The difficulty-aware design of HaloBlock smooths cross-block context propagation and lowers decoding difficulty for hard tokens, yielding better generation quality and faster convergence. Evaluated on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, Dream-7B-Instruct and LLaDA-1.5 across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, HaloBlock demonstrates consistent accuracy improvements and higher inference efficiency. Source codes are publicly available at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/HaloBlock.

Machine Learning.title: Asynchronous Sharpness-Aware Minimization For Fast and Accurate Deep Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) is an optimization method that improves the generalization performance of machine learning models. Despite its effectiveness, it has not been widely adopted in real-world applications due to its high computational cost. Existing approaches reduce this overhead by approximating or reusing gradients in the perturbation step, but still assume sequential perturbation and update steps. In this study, we introduce AsyncSAM, a variant of SAM that enables concurrent model perturbation and parameter updates across multiple compute resources. By adjusting the perturbation batch size in a system-aware manner, our asynchronous scheme fully overlaps perturbation with updates, eliminating the overhead and allowing even CPUs to perform perturbations without extra time. We also provide theoretical analysis showing that AsyncSAM achieves the same order of convergence as conventional SAM. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AsyncSAM delivers superior generalization performance and the highest training throughput among state-of-the-art SAM variants. For example, in ViT fine-tuning on CIFAR-100, it achieves accuracy comparable to SAM while maintaining training time nearly identical to SGD.

Machine Learning.title: LLM-OSDA: An Optimal-Stopping Dynamic Auction for Native Advertising in Multi-Turn LLM Conversations
Machine Learning.summary: LLM-native advertising embeds sponsored content directly into model-generated responses, shifting the unit of sale from a fixed slot to a moment within an evolving conversation. Existing LLM ad-auction mechanisms primarily operate within a single response, settling the winner but not the timing. The extension is nontrivial: with one native insertion opportunity per session, the stopping time depends on bids, coupling timing with allocation, so static truthfulness arguments no longer apply. We propose the LLM-based Optimal Stopping Dynamic Auction (LLM-OSDA), a dynamic cost-per-click auction that integrates Bellman optimal stopping, winner allocation, and envelope pricing. A bid-independent LLM layer estimates contextual click quality and seamlessly renders the winning ad, while bids enter only the committed auction mechanism. Under an exact Bellman oracle, the expected discounted-click allocation is monotone in each advertiser's bid, and the corresponding envelope payment makes truthful bidding weakly dominant in expectation. For practical deployment, a learned StopNet approximates the Bellman action values. We show that its decisions differ from the optimal policy only near the stopping boundary and bound the resulting incentive loss in terms of its approximation error. Experiments on a simulated conversational advertising corpus show that LLM-OSDA improves net revenue by 11 percent over the strongest fixed-timing baseline while maintaining comparable user retention. Code is at https://github.com/2025Fang2025/llm-osda.
Machine Learning.comment: 21 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to ACL Rolling Review (ARR), October 2026 cycle

Machine Learning.title: Process Rewards for Outcome-Guided Reasoning Steps in LLM Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary:
Mathematical reasoning in large language models has improved substantially with reinforcement learning using verifiable rewards, where final answers can be checked automatically and converted into reliable training signals. Most such pipelines optimize outcome correctness only, which yields sparse feedback for long, multi-step solutions and offers limited guidance on intermediate reasoning errors. Recent work therefore introduces process reward models (PRMs) to score intermediate steps and provide denser supervision. In practice, PRM scores are often imperfectly aligned with final correctness and can reward locally fluent reasoning that still ends in an incorrect answer. When optimized as absolute rewards, such signals can amplify fluent failure modes and induce reward hacking.
  We propose PROGRS, a framework that leverages PRMs while keeping outcome correctness dominant. PROGRS treats process rewards as relative preferences within outcome groups rather than absolute targets. We introduce outcome-conditioned centering, which shifts PRM scores of incorrect trajectories to have zero mean within each prompt group. It removes systematic bias while preserving informative rankings. PROGRS combines a frozen quantile-regression PRM with a multi-scale coherence evaluator. We integrate the resulting centered process bonus into Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) without auxiliary objectives or additional trainable components. Across MATH-500, AMC, AIME, MinervaMath, and OlympiadBench, PROGRS consistently improves Pass@1 over outcome-only baselines and achieves stronger performance with fewer rollouts. These results show that outcome-conditioned centering enables safe and effective use of process rewards for mathematical reasoning.
Machine Learning.comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables, accepted in IJCNN 2026 conference

Machine Learning.title: Sea-Net: A Small and Inherently Interpretable Neural Network for Time Series Classification
Machine Learning.summary: Traditional time-series classification methods often operate as black boxes, providing a class prediction without indicating which time point or time interval within the series led to that prediction. To improve temporal interpretability, MILLET (Multiple Instance Learning with Temporal Explanation), which combines an InceptionTime encoder with Conjunctive Pooling, provides both classification and temporal explanations. However, MILLET contains approximately 424 K parameters, making it unsuitable for deployment on resource-constrained micro-controllers, and it achieves an overall time-series accuracy of 0.888 and an explanation score of 0.681 NDCG@n. We therefore propose SEA-Net, a lightweight architecture using small multi-scale depthwise-separable convolutional TSC encoders and improved Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) pooling heads. Our SEA-Net bottleneck encoder with Top-k pooling achieves 0.931 accuracy and 0.765 NDCG@n with only 41 K parameters. Another variant, using a gated encoder with Top-k pooling, achieves 0.955 accuracy and 0.750 NDCG@n with 62 K parameters. These results demonstrate that lightweight architectures can maintain strong classification performance and temporal explanations while substantially reducing model size. The proposed variants address specific limitations of the pooling strategy used by MILLET, providing a practical direction for interpretable time-series classification on resource-constrained edge devices.

Machine Learning.title: Artifacts of Numerical Integration in Learning Dynamical Systems
Machine Learning.summary: In many applications, one needs to learn a dynamical system from its solutions sampled at a finite number of time points. The learning problem is often formulated as an optimization problem over a chosen function class. However, in the optimization procedure, prediction data from generic dynamics requires a numerical integrator to assess the mismatch with the observed data. This paper reveals potentially serious effects of a chosen numerical scheme on the learning outcome. Specifically, the analysis demonstrates that a damped oscillatory system may be incorrectly identified as having "anti-damping" and exhibiting a reversed oscillation direction, even though it adequately fits the given data points. This paper shows that the stability region of the selected integrator will distort the nature of the learned dynamics. Crucially, reducing the step size or raising the order of an explicit integrator does not, in general, remedy this artifact, because higher-order explicit methods have stability regions that extend further into the right half complex plane. Furthermore, it is shown that the implicit midpoint method can preserve either conservative or dissipative properties from discrete data, offering a principled integrator choice even when the only prior knowledge is that the system is autonomous.

Machine Learning.title: SIGMA: Symmetry-aware, Intelligent, Geometric, Multi-faced Adaptive Traffic Control for Reliable Intelligent Transportation Systems
Machine Learning.summary: Traffic signal control is a challenging sequential decision-making problem requiring a balance between throughput, vehicle delay fairness, signal stability, predictable switching, and emergency vehicle prioritisation. Existing reinforcement learning (RL) approaches often rely on predefined objectives and offer limited adaptability to changing operational priorities. They may also generalise poorly across geometrically equivalent intersections. To address these limitations, SIGMA (Symmetry-aware, Intelligent, Geometric, Multi-faced Adaptive traffic control) is proposed as a multi-faced RL framework augmented with a large language model (LLM) for dynamic objective adaptation and orientation-invariant policy learning. Natural language emergency instructions are translated into priority vectors that guide a multi-faced actor-critic controller. Symmetry-aware rotational augmentation supports transfer across homogeneous four-way intersections, while an offline-to-online learning strategy enables stable initialisation and adaptation to evolving traffic conditions. Structural properties concerning emergency service levels, graceful degradation under LLM failure, and sensitivity to traffic demand perturbations are established, alongside bootstrap-based statistical validation. Experiments in SUMO across four urban intersections modelled on Kolkata traffic scenarios compare SIGMA with fixed-time, actuated, and Deep Q-Network controllers. Reductions in average waiting times, emergency waiting times, and queue lengths are observed, alongside improved traffic throughput. Empirical reliability and ablation analyses further assess robustness to component failures and geometric orientation. SIGMA integrates language-guided objective adaptation, multi-faced policy learning, and statistical reliability assessment into an adaptive framework for intelligent traffic control.

Machine Learning.title: Stein Variational Distributional Reinforcement Learning: Score-Guided Particles for Multivariate Return Distributions
Machine Learning.summary: Decisions that weigh several reward signals against each other require the joint distribution of the return vector. Categorical critics scale exponentially in the reward dimension, and quantiles have no canonical multivariate analogue. Multivariate distributional critics therefore represent each return distribution by M equal-weight particles trained with a discrepancy loss. Beyond their atoms, the particles provide no sampler and cannot resolve events rarer than 1/M. We propose Stein variational distributional RL (SVDRL). Its critic outputs Stein particles, which Stein variational gradient descent transports along a learned score field of the distributional Bellman target. We learn this field by bootstrapped denoising score matching across noise levels and tie it across the Bellman recursion by a consistency loss, which we prove is a non-expansive temporal-difference scheme in score space. The same field certifies the particles. Its reverse-diffusion sampler satisfies a supremal Wasserstein policy-evaluation bound that holds for bounded, possibly multimodal returns. The Stein particles inherit this bound up to a gap that we measure without ground truth, and the sampler answers tail-risk queries below the particle resolution at any sample size. Empirically, SVDRL is more accurate on rare events than particle critics with the same number of particles, and on par on MuJoCo continuous control.

Machine Learning.title: NBCLT: Parameter-Agnostic Norm-Ball Clipped Local Training
Machine Learning.summary: Distributed learning with multiple local steps reduces communication but aggravates drift, and its practical performance often depends on carefully tuned hyperparameters under heterogeneous data and communication constraints. At the same time, recent Muon-type optimizers suggest that constraining updates within suitable norm balls provides a simple way to encode geometric priors into optimization. In this work, we propose NBCLT (Norm-Ball Clipped Local Training), a unified local-training framework for both federated learning (FL) and decentralized learning (DL). NBCLT combines a predict-and-correct local update rule with Euclidean projections onto flexible norm balls, thereby performing norm-ball clipping under flexible update geometries while retaining a simple implementation. In FL, its problem-parameter-free regime achieves $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2})$ communication complexity and $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-4})$ total stochastic-gradient complexity without assuming bounded heterogeneity, when the per-round local-computation budget is scaled appropriately with the horizon. In DL, NBCLT is compatible with both static and time-varying mixing and preserves these accuracy exponents under the analogous computation scaling, up to fixed network constants and an additive initialization cost.

Machine Learning.title: AdNGCL: Adaptive Negative Scheduling for Graph Contrastive Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Negative samples play a crucial role in graph contrastive learning (GCL), yet existing methods mainly focus on which negatives should be selected, mined, filtered, or progressively introduced. Less attention has been given to separating the negative candidates available to an anchor from the subset that actively participates in optimization, and to adapting this exposure according to training behavior. To address this gap, we propose the Adaptive Negative Scheduling for Graph Contrastive Learning (AdNGCL) framework, which maintains a bounded per-anchor candidate reservoir and periodically reassesses candidate hardness as representations evolve. Its core component, Hardness-Aware Negative Scheduling (HANS), uses a category-specific training-response signal to determine whether exposure to easy, intermediate, or hard negatives should increase at each scheduling opportunity. Furthermore, reliability-aware candidate refresh handles potentially positive-like candidates, while within-category diversity refresh changes active identities without altering HANS-controlled exposure. AdNGCL retains a standard symmetric InfoNCE objective. Experiments on ten benchmark datasets against state-of-the-art self-supervised graph learning methods show that AdNGCL achieves the highest mean Micro-F1 among the evaluated methods on eight datasets, with improvements of up to 1.30 percentage points over the second-best method, ranks second on Actor, and remains competitive on Coauthor-CS. Ablation, sensitivity, scheduler and reliability diagnostics, and computational analyses further examine the behavior and contribution of the proposed mechanisms.
Machine Learning.comment: Substantially revised methodology and experimental evaluation. Updated HANS scheduling and candidate-management mechanisms, independently evaluated baselines under a unified evaluation protocol, and expanded ablation, sensitivity, and computational analyses

Machine Learning.title: JaGNet: Detection, Identification and Position Error Correction of GNSS Jamming with Deep Temporal Graphs
Machine Learning.summary: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) underpin location-dependent mobile computing, such as railway signaling, public transport and fleet tracking, yet face growing disruption from low-cost jammers. Under moderate jamming, low-cost receivers keep reporting a valid fix, shifted by up to several meters and often without an interference flag. Their built-in defenses run in closed firmware, and existing data-driven position error correction methods are designed for multipath, require raw pseudoranges or operate on single epochs. We propose JaGNet, a single-layer heterogeneous graph convolutional LSTM over star graphs of the receiver and its satellites, which, from the standard receiver output alone, detects the jamming, identifies its type and power, and corrects the reported position only when jamming is detected. We evaluate it on new hardware-in-the-loop recordings of a commercial multi-constellation receiver under three jammer types at six powers, at six static locations and on eleven railway and bus routes. JaGNet detects 99.8 to 99.9% of the jammed 10-s windows with at most 1.0% false positives, against 64.7 to 66.2% for the receiver's own monitor, and identifies the jammer type in 95.2 to 96.6% of them. Trained in the laboratory only, it detects 97.7% of the Jammertest 2024 field windows with a C/N0 drop of 10 dB or more. It reduces the mean absolute position error by 67.5% at held-out locations and by 64.0% on held-out route repetitions, where its error is 20.2 cm below that of the strongest baseline, whereas at the static locations the attention-based baselines are within 0.4 cm of it.

Machine Learning.title: Stable-Plastic Subspace Construction for Differentially Private Continual LoRA
Machine Learning.summary: Continual learning (CL) adapts pretrained models to a sequence of tasks while retaining knowledge acquired from earlier tasks. When task data are sensitive, differential privacy (DP) provides record-level protection, but maintaining both adaptation and retention under privacy constraints remains challenging. We study this problem in continual low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and observe that: 1) private training increases forgetting primarily during subsequent adaptation rather than initial task acquisition; 2) jointly perturbing both LoRA factors introduces a non-negligible bilinear noise interaction; and 3) DP aggravates the stability-plasticity dilemma, hindering both knowledge retention and adaptation to new tasks. Based on these observations, we propose DP-SPA, which constructs a stable subspace from previously privatized updates and a plastic subspace from pretrained weights within its orthogonal complement. The method fixes these bases and privately optimizes only the LoRA factor, eliminating the bilinear noise interaction within each step. Before merging each task update, it rescales stable-direction coefficients using historical and current update energies. We establish a privacy guarantee and show that recalibration does not increase historical overlap and tightens a conditional upper bound on old-task loss increase. Experiments across five datasets, eight settings, and multiple privacy budgets show that DP-SPA improves average accuracy and reduces forgetting compared with the evaluated baselines.

Machine Learning.title: FlashMask-3: Efficient and Expressive Mask-Aware Distributed Attention
Machine Learning.summary: Long-context training of large language and multimodal models couples structured attention masks (document, prefix-LM, share-question, sliding-window, block-sparse) with multi-node context parallelism, making the mask a dominant bottleneck. FlashMask's column-wise sparse mask compresses them from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$ via four query-axis boundary vectors, covering broad structured patterns. Implemented for Ampere GPUs, it neither exploits FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA warp-specialized pipeline on Hopper nor supports distribution. The column-wise sparse mask is indexed by key positions but stores query-axis interval boundaries. Under any multi-chunk context-parallel assignment, it reduces per-rank mask localization to a provably zero-communication \emph{clip--shift--max} on the boundary vectors, compatible with the single-GPU kernel. FlashMask-3 introduces a mask-aware Hopper kernel with three-role warp specialization atop FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA pipeline, plus a mask-aware distributed extension: zero-communication mask localization, a sparsity-aware load balancer (HCC-IPO), and a mask-aware compute-communication overlap with mask-driven communication pruning, whose forward all-gather uses topology-aware hierarchical routing. On a single H100 across 12 masks at 4K--128K context, it improves achieved TFLOPs over FlashMask, FlexAttention, and MagiAttention by 45--141%, 34--71%, and 2--44%. At context-parallel degrees 4--32 with 8K sequence per device, it attains 31--75% compute-communication overlap efficiency and improves throughput over Megatron-Core CP ring, Megatron-Core CP all-gather, and MagiAttention by $1.80\times$--$3.71\times$, $1.71\times$--$2.92\times$, and $1.09\times$--$1.46\times$. In end-to-end training of a 118B-A14B MoE at 128K on 128 H100 GPUs, it raises throughput by 7.3--11.0% over a Dual Chunk all-gather baseline, with attention forward+backward 24.5--44.9% faster.
Machine Learning.comment: Published as a main conference paper at NeurIPS 2026

Machine Learning.title: PaceReasoner: Label-Free Learning to Answer Briefly from Long Reasoning
Machine Learning.summary: Extended chain-of-thought reasoning improves problem-solving performance but increases inference cost and latency, motivating more accurate answers with shorter reasoning. We introduce PaceReasoner, a label-free test-time reinforcement learning framework that uses a model's LONG responses to improve its SHORT-mode accuracy. Both modes share a trainable policy, creating a need for reliable supervision, sufficient SHORT training samples, and continued LONG responses to guide learning. PaceReasoner combines all-response and LONG-only answer consensus through progressive, confidence-weighted supervision. A behavior reward gradually shifts from encouraging SHORT exploration to rewarding agreement with LONG answers, while a ratio controller regulates the balance between modes. Across three model backbones and four benchmarks, PaceReasoner improves average SHORT accuracy over the baselines by 7.4--13.5 percentage points, with fewer than 25 reasoning tokens per response on average. Ablations support the key components, and cross-dataset results demonstrate transfer beyond the adaptation set.

Machine Learning.title: Evaluating the Causal Faithfulness of SHAP as a Candidate Attribution Method for SAE Features
Machine Learning.summary: Sparse autoencoders decompose language model representations into interpretable features, but feature interpretation in this literature remains predominantly correlational. Attribution methods offer more direct estimates of feature influence, yet their faithfulness to actual causal effects has not been systematically evaluated in the SAE setting. We apply SHAP-based attribution to SAE latent features and evaluate it against direct causal intervention, using sentiment classification on SST-2 with GPT-2 Small and a 32,768-feature layer-7 SAE as a testbed. We compare SHAP to Integrated Gradients, Gradient$\times$Input, and probe-weight baselines across linear and MLP probe arms, scoring each against feature ablation and activation steering measured through the language model's own logit difference. Most faithfulness associations we measure do not survive multiple-comparison correction, and attribution methods that agree strongly with one another ($ρ= 0.42$--$0.80$) agree poorly with measured causal effects, indicating that inter-method agreement is not evidence of causal faithfulness. Two effects hold under control. First, local per-example attribution retains a directional advantage over global averaged attribution, while its apparent importance advantage is explained by feature activity rather than superior causal ranking. Second, under known-ground-truth minimal pairs, attribution recovers inserted sentiment signal well above chance (AUROC $0.792$) but fails to localize deletions (AUROC $0.520$), suggesting that these methods detect the presence of a feature's influence more reliably than its absence. We argue that importance faithfulness and directional faithfulness are separable properties requiring separate evaluation, and that attribution agreement should not substitute for causal validation.
Machine Learning.comment: 24 pages, 3 figures; to be submitted to International Journal of Secondary Computing and Applications Research

Machine Learning.title: Blackknife: Query-Free Black-Box Rewiring Attacks on Heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks
Machine Learning.summary: Heterogeneous graph neural networks (HGNNs) perform well on graphs with multiple node and relation types, but their robustness to attacks with restricted structural access remains insufficiently understood. We propose Blackknife, a query-free, strict black-box evasion attack that observes only the one-hop structures of the attacked nodes, their ground-truth labels, and raw features within the permitted action space. No victim-model outputs are used to train the surrogate, generate perturbations, or select attacks.Blackknife trains a shared surrogate using only observable edges and relation types, then optimizes structural perturbations through continuous relaxation and projected gradient ascent. Each rewiring operation deletes one edge and adds another of the same relation type, preserving the target node's total degree and degree for each relation type. A cosine-similarity penalty and an adaptive structural classifier further regularize the perturbations through bilevel optimization. Experiments on different datasets demonstrate competitive attack success rates across five victim architectures and three defense settings. The results expose HGNN vulnerabilities under jointly restricted graph access and query-free attack generation.

Machine Learning.title: Fitted Q-Iteration with Continuous Actions and Adaptive Data: Smoothed Coverage and Minimax Rates
Machine Learning.summary: Fitted Q-iteration (FQI) is well understood when the data come from a fixed distribution and the action set is finite, whereas value-based continuous control collects its data adaptively and maximizes over continuous actions. Both features break the standard analysis: the regression data are dependent, and every density-ratio concentrability coefficient of a deterministic greedy policy is infinite when the exploration has no atoms. Conditioning on the history freezes the regression target, so each round of FQI is a regression with martingale noise, and we obtain localized rates that are fast for classes of polylogarithmic metric entropy. We transfer the regression error to the loss of the greedy policy by smoothing the measures on which this loss is evaluated, at a price that depends on the action dimension and the smoothness of the residuals in the action. Under deterministic dynamics the state is smoothed as well, and the state dimension enters the price. Minimax lower bounds with the same exponents in the sample size show that no learner avoids these prices, for restart data in the case of the state dimension. The coverage conditions do not involve the unknown greedy policies; they hold under exploration floors with restarts and, for action smoothing, bounded transition densities.

Machine Learning.title: Interaction-as-a-Judge
Machine Learning.summary: Coding agents are tasked with producing sophisticated interactive applications such as websites, desktop applications, and games. While humans assess these applications interactively, current automated LLM evaluations primarily focus on code analysis and unit tests. This mismatch can cause LLM judges to miss failures that are immediately apparent to human users. We study Interaction-as-a-Judge, an evaluation paradigm where computer-use agents (CUAs) directly interact with an application. We demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can improve both \emph{evaluation} and \emph{generation} of interactive applications. To this end, we collect and release two complementary datasets: $6,858$ pairs of applications with human preferences and corresponding agent traces, and $222$ applications with human-verified requirement labels. Relative to standard non-interactive approaches, we find that Interaction-as-a-Judge improves evaluation in terms of predicting human preferences ($65.6\% \to 69.1\%$) and requirement verification ($77.0\% \to 81.6\%$). We also observe scaling benefits: across both preference alignment and requirement verification, higher-quality interactions improve performance. Finally, through both inference- and training-time experiments, we demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can also improve the quality of generated artifacts. At inference time, Interaction-as-a-Judge repairs $75.5\%$ of broken requirements within five attempts, compared to $55.4\%$ for code-only self-feedback. At training time, using Interaction-as-a-Judge as a reward signal improves win-rate over the base model by $6.7$pp while reducing both generated code length by $35.7\%$ and build failure rates by $7.2$pp compared to a code-only reward signal.

Machine Learning.title: Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards
Machine Learning.summary: Effective collaboration among large language model (LLM) agents in multi-agent systems requires sharing relevant evidence, requesting missing information, and incorporating teammates' contributions into decisions. Training these behaviors is challenging because final task outcomes provide limited feedback on the value of individual messages. We introduce CoSIR (Collaboration via Surprisal-based Information Rewards), a post-training approach that uses a simple, verifiable environment to teach collaboration behaviors that generalize to more complex, unseen tasks. We propose a Bayesian evaluator that scores shared information by its reduction in team surprisal, defined as the sum of the negative log probabilities assigned to the correct option given each agent's available evidence. Requests are scored by the potential reduction in the same quantity if the requested information were truthfully provided. Separate rewards encourage agents to use the received information in their private choices and calculations. We post-train Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-3-4B-it through self-play and evaluate transfer to seven unseen natural-language collaboration tasks. CoSIR achieves the highest aggregate score, while its performance in general tasks remains competitive. Behavioral analyses show increased disclosure of private evidence and fewer judged failures to use teammates' input.

Machine Learning.title: Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics
