We demonstrate CIViC on actor-disjoint face-raster tests, a synthetic audio-feature mixture, and source-video-disjoint SpeakerVid proxy tasks. In the static face-raster test, cross-actor audio replacement meets the registered detection rule with a small effect; on a separate temporal endpoint, constant-audio fits score better than audio-trained fits in four matched seeds. In the synthetic mixture, the condition-augmented fit has higher 1,000-step RMSE than the audio-only fit (0.1807 vs. 0.1707), with the gap shrinking during training. In the SpeakerVid proxy, the five-feature-zero fit (five low-level audio summaries zeroed; identity, dialogue, and condition inputs retained) has lower whole-frame grayscale RMSE than aligned audio across four held-out conditions and five paired seeds, while aligned audio has lower segment-drift error. The results show that output activation, held-out error, and endpoint controls support different interpretations across these proxy tasks.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Pixels to Tokens: Token Space Efficient Active Learning for Low-Budget Semantic Segmentation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: While foundation models and vision transformers (ViTs) have redefined visual representations, current active learning (AL) strategies for these backbones largely operate at the patch or region level, where annotation requirements remain high due to extensive pixel labeling. Extending ViT-based AL to the pixel-level, low-budget regime is uniquely challenging: with as little as one pixel query per image, a method must simultaneously identify the most informative locations and train a reliable decoder head from an extremely sparse signal. We introduce TEAL (Token-space Efficient Active Learning), the first pixel-level AL framework built around ViT representations. TEAL uses a frozen ViT backbone and performs diversity-based selection directly on its native token lattice, avoiding the artifacts introduced by interpolating token embeddings to dense pixel resolutions. Our framework applies a two-level MaxHerding strategy over multi-layer token descriptors to select representative candidates, followed by margin-based uncertainty refinement on a finer decoder grid. Across CamVid, Cityscapes, ADE20K, and Pascal Context, TEAL consistently outperforms previous baselines under extreme label scarcity, improving over the strongest baseline by up to +24.36 mIoU with a single labeled pixel (px) per image, and reaching up to 97% of fully supervised performance with just 10 px. To rigorously establish the source of the gains, we further show that the improvements persist when all baselines are equipped with the same DINOv3 backbone, demonstrating that coupling token-space selection with uncertainty refinement on the decoder grid makes ViT token geometry an effective foundation for extremely low-budget active segmentation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: DefoliationCAM: An Edge-AI System for Real-Time Insect Defoliation Severity Assessment in Grapevines
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Insect-induced defoliation threatens grapevine health and yield, yet severity assessment relies on subjective manual scouting. We developed DefoliationCAM (D-CAM), a solar-powered edge AI system that estimates canopy defoliation and transmits results via LoRa to a web dashboard. The pipeline uses YOLOX-Nano to localize grapevine cordons in 4K images and a MobileNet-based classifier with lightweight channel attention to classify 320 x 320 pixel patches. The 29,674 field-collected patches were labeled as background or one of four damage levels: no to negligible, mild, moderate, and severe. Merging moderate and severe classes reduced the class imbalance ratio from approximately 40:1 to 8.8:1. Synthetic augmentation increased macro-F1 from 0.768 to 0.838. The classifier outperformed ResNet-50 in macro-F1 with fewer parameters (1.08 M versus 23.52 M). Patch predictions were aggregated into a canopy-level Non-linear Global Defoliation Severity (NGDS) score and validated against an entomologist's ratings of 86 held-out canopy images. Quadratic discriminant analysis identified boundaries of 9% and 29% separating negligible damage, mild damage requiring monitoring, and action-level damage warranting on-site scouting and insecticide treatment consideration. The 29% boundary aligned with the 25%-30% action threshold range for Japanese beetle management in grapevine. Using TensorRT FP16 on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, the pipeline processed each 4K image in approximately 1.5 s, with a complete operating cycle of 57-60 s. A five-week deployment of two field units demonstrated the feasibility of autonomous solar-powered operation, LoRa communication, and remote defoliation monitoring. D-CAM supports frequent, objective canopy damage assessment for targeted scouting and timely pest-management decisions.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Probing Negation Understanding in Vision-Language Models With Object Attention
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Negation is a fundamental aspect of language understanding and it is important vision-language models (VLMs) are able to process it effectively. We investigate how VLMs process negation by analysing attention patterns of different models. We draw comparisons between human gaze and attention in models when processing affirmative vs negated statements. We compare object level model attention to human eye-fixations in both binary and multary settings, evaluating with both synthetic and realistic datasets. We find models generally do not follow human-like attention patterns when resolving negation, suggesting they rely on mechanisms outside of attention. While layerwise analysis shows that PaliGemma2-3B shifts object attention to the alternative under negation, our headwise ablations suggest this is a byproduct rather than a negation processing mechanism. Additionally, we find that LLaVA-1.5-7B displays a spatial bias towards left-side objects. Our evaluation of models on downstream tasks shows that all models have a discrepancy between affirmative and negated questions highlighting the need to better understand the underlying processing of negation to close this performance gap. Code available at https://github.com/otmive/negation_attention

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: MARS - A foundational map auto-regressor
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Map generation tasks feature extensive non-structural vectorized data (e.g., points, polylines, and polygons) and thus pose significant challenges to common pixel-wise generative models. Conventional approaches use multiple stages, first segmenting these features at the pixel level and then performing vectorized post-processing, with errors and complexity compounding at each stage. Motivated by the recent success of auto-regressive language modeling, we propose the first map foundation model, named Map Auto-Regressor (MARS), that is capable of generating both multi-polyline road networks and polygon buildings in a unified manner. For training MARS, we collected to our knowledge the largest multi-class map extraction dataset totaling 3.4M examples, which we call MAP-3M. Across four road and building datasets, MARS outperforms or matches the performance of multistage baselines. Additionally, we develop a "Chat with MARS" capability that enables interactive human-in-the-loop map generation and correction, supported by the auto-regressive nature of our end-to-end approach. We release our MAP-3M dataset and project demo page at (1) https://huggingface.co/datasets/bag-lab/MAP-3M and (2) https://huggingface.co/spaces/bag-lab/MARS, respectively.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: LightMedSeg-ISLES: Stroke Lesion Segmentation with 81x Fewer Parameters than nnU-Net
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Large networks and ensembles often lead medical image segmentation challenges, but their storage and inference demands complicate deployment. We present LightMedSeg-ISLES, a 1.26-million-parameter pipeline for T1-weighted stroke lesion segmentation in ISLES'26. On a 146-case held-out cohort, flip test-time augmentation produces 0.618 mean Dice and 0.599 lesion-wise F1. A 102.35-million-parameter nnU-Net ResEnc-L produces 0.634 Dice and 0.544 lesion-wise F1 after size filtering. LightMedSeg therefore retains 97.5\% of nnU-Net's Dice with 81.4$\times$ fewer parameters while improving lesion-wise F1 by 0.055. Its four-pass TTA operating point requires 4.7$\times$ fewer FLOPs per standardized patch than nnU-Net. It also slightly exceeds filtered UNETR++ and nnFormer. Longer training and stronger augmentation add 0.0358 Dice without increasing capacity, establishing a strong single-checkpoint alternative to much larger models.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to ISLES 2026 challenge. To be published in Springer Lecture Notes in Computer Science (LNCS) as part of the SWITCH+ 2026 workshop proceedings

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Temporal Specification Guidance for Text-to-Video Generation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Text-to-video models often generate the visual concepts requested in natural language prompts but fail to satisfy their intended ordering, timing, and persistence requirements. We propose representing these requirements as specifications in a formal Temporal Logic, and introduce Temporal Specification Guidance (TSG), a training-free inference-time framework that turns temporal specifications into executable objectives for guiding video generation during sampling. TSG scores traces of visual concept evidence using differentiable quantitative semantics and uses the score's gradients to construct a specification-guided denoising direction. We instantiate this framework with video-text attention traces, efficient differentiable scores for Metric Temporal Logic, and gradient-derived attention biases. This instantiation requires neither an external concept classifier nor backpropagation through the video transformer. Its attention-steered forward pass yields a denoising direction that augments classifier-free guidance (CFG). On a benchmark of 220 prompts spanning 11 categories of temporal constraints, including ordered object entry and state transitions, this instantiation improves specification satisfaction accuracy over CFG by 9.5-20 percentage points across five models, with minimal memory overhead. These results demonstrate the potential of temporal specifications and differentiable satisfaction objectives as a flexible interface for controlling video generation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Meaningful Moments: A Corpus of VLM-Derived Temporal Importance Labels for Video Action Recognition
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Not every moment in a video is equally useful for recognizing an action. A few decisive moments often carry the evidence: the instant an object moves, the peak of a dive, or one object placed on another. Existing video datasets rarely provide large-scale, action-conditioned labels for which short segments carry that evidence. This work asks whether vision-language models can identify meaningful moments at scale and whether those labels improve action recognition. We introduce Meaningful Moments (MM), a corpus of about 4.58 million VLM-generated per-segment importance scores for nearly 500,000 class-labeled videos spanning Something-Something v2 (SSv2), Kinetics-400 (K400), and Diving-48 across 622 action classes. We freeze the action classifier and vary only temporal sampling. An alpha-parameterized comparison of importance-led selection against an importance-inverted control separates gains from the VLM signal from gains caused by variable-density sampling alone. Across all three datasets, VLM-derived importance is informative: at the hard-cut endpoint, keeping VLM-important segments outperforms keeping VLM-designated filler. Usefulness depends on class structure. On Diving-48, importance-led fast-forwarding preserves full-video recognition while the inverted control collapses by roughly 30 percentage points. On K400, hard-cut selection beats uniform sampling by 1.45 percentage points, rising to 2.05 under threshold selection. On SSv2, the labels carry signal but do not recover full-video performance. Direct scoring matches greedy removal within its noise floor at roughly 25 times fewer oracle calls, and a four-VLM cross-oracle study shows consistent downstream trends. We release the importance labels and evaluation protocol under CC-BY-4.0; SSv2 class strings remain under CC-BY-NC-4.0.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to WACV 2027. Supplementary material included

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Intern Lumina U2: A Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Unified multimodal generation covers discrete, continuous, and hybrid paradigms. Discrete approaches with single-codebook visual tokenizers align naturally with text modeling but have limited representational capacity. Continuous and hybrid approaches retain richer visual representations, but they model text and images in heterogeneous spaces with different training objectives, potentially introducing optimization conflicts between modalities with misaligned representation spaces. These choices expose a central question: how to efficiently model high-capacity visual representations alongside textual content in a shared optimization space within a single backbone. We present Intern Lumina U2, to our knowledge the first diffusion language model to represent multi-codebook visual tokens in a fully discrete space. Each visual position is represented by a group of codes from complementary codebooks, increasing its representational capacity while preserving compatibility with discrete text modeling. At the input, the embeddings are concatenated at each position; at the output, a lightweight multi-codebook autoregressive head predicts the codes within each position sequentially, while the diffusion backbone processes all positions in parallel. Built on the unified 4D representation of AToken, Intern Lumina U2 supports image, video, and 3D inputs within a single backbone and achieves leading performance among unified models in visual understanding, image generation, and image editing. We further build a full-stack training, inference, and evaluation system on both Ascend and NVIDIA platforms to verify the cross-platform effectiveness of our model. We also improve the inference efficiency through a stability-aware sampling strategy, which combines confidence-plateau-guided unmasking approach with drift-triggered cache refreshing mechanisms, accelerating image generation by 4.45x.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Benchmarking Efficient & Effective Camera Pose Estimation Strategies for Novel View Synthesis
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Novel view synthesis (NVS) approaches such as NeRFs or 3DGS can produce photo-realistic 3D scene representation from a set of images with known extrinsic and intrinsic parameters. The necessary camera poses and calibrations are typically obtained from the images via Structure-from-Motion (SfM). Classical SfM approaches rely on local feature matches between the images to estimate both the poses and a sparse 3D model of the scene, using bundle adjustment to refine initial pose, intrinsics, and geometry estimates. In order to increase run-time efficiency, recent SfM systems forgo optimization via bundle adjustment. Instead, they train feed-forward (transformer-based) neural networks to directly regress camera parameters and the 3D structure. While orders of magnitude more efficient, such recent works produce significantly less accurate estimates. To stimulate research on developing SfM approaches that are both efficient and effective, this paper develops a benchmark focused on SfM for novel view synthesis. Using existing datasets and two simple strategies for making the reconstruction process more efficient, we show that: (1) simply using fewer features already significantly accelerates classical SfM methods while maintaining high pose accuracy. (2) using feed-forward networks to obtain initial estimates and refining them using classical SfM techniques leads to the best efficiency-effectiveness trade-off. Our benchmark and code are publicly available at https://github.com/jhacsonmeza/sfm-benchmark-nvs.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Accepted to the Structure-from-Motion in the Age of Deep Learning Workshop at ECCV 2026

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: RIGen: Beyond Action Following with Reciprocal Interaction in Generative Gameplay
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Generative gameplay requires more than immediate responses to player actions.Actions should have persistent consequences, while the generated world should act according to its own state and rules, shaping the player's situation and subsequent choices. Video generation captures local dynamics, but limited history, partially observed game state, and the need for contextual behavior decisions make such interactions difficult to sustain through audiovisual prediction alone. We introduce \rig (Reciprocally Interactive Generation), a framework for reciprocal interaction in generative gameplay. \rig combines persistent state and configurable rules, contextual interaction reasoning, and action-conditioned audiovisual generation. Together, these components make interaction consequences and actor behavior jointly determine generated content while maintaining consistency between game state and visible outcomes. We construct a Xonotic gameplay dataset to train an audiovisual generator for learning dynamics and interactions. Further post-training enables \rigarena, an interactive generative first-person shooter (FPS) prototype. Experiments demonstrate more reliable combat outcomes and reciprocal interaction between the player and the generated world. Project page: https://murphylmf.github.io/RIGen/.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Blame Errant Words, Not the Canvas: Defect-Aware Spatial Credit Assignment for Visual Text Generation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Recent reinforcement learning approaches have improved visual text generation, yet generated images still suffer from incorrect wording and malformed glyphs. We identify two coupled limitations: recognition-based rewards often overlook visible glyph defects, while whole-image scalar feedback obscures the uneven quality of individual text regions. These limitations motivate our central principle: $\textit{Blame errant words, not the canvas}$, to effectively preserve local quality distinctions. First, we introduce $\mathbf{TextDART}$, a defect-aware region-targeted reward model that localizes individual text regions and independently evaluates their semantic correctness and glyph quality, providing fine-grained, region-precise feedback. Building on TextDART, we propose $\mathbf{SCANNER}$, which turns these regional judgments into spatially differentiated policy feedback. It normalizes rewards for each text target across sampled images and casts the resulting regional advantages onto the corresponding latent tokens. Extensive experiments on existing benchmarks and our newly established $\textbf{PolyText-Bench}$ demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in text accuracy and glyph fidelity. Project page: https://sujiehu.github.io/textdart-scanner

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: ReasonUni: Reasoning-Augmented Reconstruction Advances Unified Multimodal Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Image-to-text (I2T) understanding and text-to-image (T2I) generation are dual tasks in unified multimodal models (UMMs). Reconstructive post-training couples these tasks, but existing reconstruction-based methods remain perception-centric and provide limited supervision for reasoning about structure, intent, and transformation. We propose ReasonUni, a reasoning-augmented reconstructive post-training framework that extends this coupling beyond perception. Given an original image and an editing instruction, the UMM first reasons about what and how to edit and describes the target state, then generates the corresponding target image conditioned on this understanding output. To jointly optimize both modules, we introduce TreeGRPO, a tree-structured reinforcement learning method that samples multiple reasoning paths and candidate images per path, then aggregates visual rewards to update both modules under a unified objective. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate consistent gains in both understanding and generation, showing that reasoning-augmented reconstruction yields genuine mutual gains for UMMs.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Evaluating the Semantic-to-Geometric Gap in Adversarial Defenses Against Vision-Language Model-Based Plagiarism
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: The rapidly advancing capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) present a systemic challenge to academic integrity. VLMs now allow students to bypass meaningful engagement by capturing and submitting graphical problems as singular images, a practice we define as trivial plagiarism. To provide educators with actionable data on VLM limitations, we investigate the efficacy of heuristic adversarial image transformations designed to degrade model performance while remaining human-interpretable. Through a two-phase evaluation of introductory assessments, we manually assess baseline VLM performance on circuit diagrams, followed by an automated large-scale evaluation of topological structures (logic gates) and coordinate geometry (Karnaugh maps). We find that while highly capable VLMs can exhibit appreciable robustness, all models suffer vulnerability to adversarial perturbations. We conclude that while visual perturbations act as a viable near-term stopgap, long-term assessment security requires educators to reapproach assessment design given continually increasing VLM performance.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 10 Pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. To be published in the proceedings of the 60th Hawaii International Conference on System Science. Minor edit to author email address

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: A comparative assessment of global building and settlement datasets across geographic and settlement contexts
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Global building and settlement products increasingly support population mapping, exposure assessment, and urban monitoring, yet comparative evidence remains fragmented across representations, geographic contexts, and evaluation methods. We benchmark seven global or near-global products against harmonized reference building footprints across 135 study areas. Our representation-aware framework integrates complementary measures of detection, geometric agreement, and aggregate quantity accuracy with stratified analyses of settlement characteristics, evaluation resolution, reference provenance, and temporal alignment. Overture Maps achieved the highest median city-level vector F1 (0.786), while 3D-GloBFP showed the closest aggregate building-area agreement despite weaker detection performance. Raster rankings were scale-dependent: Google Open Buildings Temporal (OBT) performed best at 10\,m (F1 = 0.680), whereas WSF Tracker led at 100\,m (F1 = 0.904) but substantially overestimated reference building area (relative bias = 1.845). Raster accuracy increased with building density ($ρ=0.58$--$0.75$), while smaller candidate footprints were disproportionately associated with vector false positives. Temporal alignment improved WSF Tracker mean city-level F1 by 0.060. These findings demonstrate that product reliability depends on representation, spatial scale, and settlement context, providing a reproducible framework for assessing the suitability of EO-derived urban information for different applications.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Image Tokenizers Should Be Trained Between Images
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Latent diffusion models generate images as codes of an image tokenizer, whose decoder turns them into the pixel image. Recent tokenizers improve how well these codes reconstruct an image and how easily a generator learns them. Yet a generator does not reproduce the codes of training images, and when a generated code lands outside what the decoder expects, the decoded image contains imperfections. Current methods make the decoder more robust to generated codes by adding noise during training. However, generated codes lie between the training codes and resemble their mixture more than one of them plus noise. To improve generated images, decoders should therefore be trained on codes in the space between training samples. We propose InterpTok, which fine-tunes MAETok to decode mixtures of image codes into natural images. Since no target image exists between two training samples, a discriminator judges whether each decoded mixture looks as natural as its two sources. A mixing ratio loss requires the decoded mixture to keep the mixing ratio of the two codes. Together, they prevent collapse to a trivial solution and yield a sharp and natural composition of both images. InterpTok keeps MAETok's reconstruction quality and improves interpolation quality more than threefold, the best of all tokenizers in a recent benchmark. Beyond interpolation, InterpTok improves the generation FID of a matched diffusion transformer from 11.61 to 8.48 without guidance, and even reaches 8.11 at an eighth of the sampling steps, where the generator on MAETok's codes worsens. The generator trained on our tokenizer also reaches the final result of the one trained on MAETok at half the training steps. Our findings show that the space between image codes can and should be explicitly supervised rather than ignored.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Purify Before You Align: Improving Representation Alignment for Diffusion Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Representation alignment improves and accelerates diffusion training by encouraging intermediate features to match a pretrained visual encoder. However, standard alignment matches pretrained representations without distinguishing what information may be more useful for generation. We introduce local appearance purification (LAP), which improves generation quality and makes encoders such as MAE more effective alignment targets by removing locally predictable content and aligning to the residual. LAP modifies only the alignment target, and requires no changes to diffusion training or inference. Through controlled interventions within a fixed encoder, we show that effective alignment depends on what information the target emphasizes, not simply how much image information it contains. Our theory gives a variational interpretation of standard alignment and, for fixed local predictors, a sum of token-wise information bounds conditioned on local appearance. To understand why purification benefits some encoders more than others, we derive an exact constant-readout test that measures how well the target can be matched without using the diffusion model's hidden state. LAP improves generation quality across five pretrained representations (MAE, AIMv2, CLIP, DINOv2, DINOv3), with the largest gain for MAE: on ImageNet-256 with SiT-B/2, it reduces FID from $53.1$ to $42.3$. Its gains persist with stronger alignment recipes and tokenizers. Computed before diffusion training, the constant-readout score predicts the benefit of purification (Spearman $ρ=0.94$ across 13 encoders).
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Code and checkpoints are on the project page: https://yingheng-wang.com/LAP

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: WorldCast: Exploring Intelligent Visual Generation in World State Prediction
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Humans interpret multimodal observations of the world and forecast how it will evolve. Recent multimodal generative systems have demonstrated similar capabilities: they can integrate multimodal context and synthesize visual outputs that depict changes in the world. To characterize this emerging trajectory, we organize model capabilities into a four-level hierarchy and discover that higher-level tasks remain relatively underexplored despite model progress. To bridge this gap, we explore model performance on multi-step world state prediction, a high-level task that requires models to forecast successive future world states from multimodal observations and diverse references. Such a task requires models to possess entangled understanding and generation capabilities, as well as extensive world knowledge to translate human action sequences, physical transformations, and abstract visual reasoning into coherent visual outputs. We introduce WorldCast, a benchmark comprising 320 manually designed cases across eight categories, and evaluate 12 representative models. The conducted experiments yield three key insights: (a) advances in frontier models are rapidly pushing the boundaries of intelligent world modeling, with the GPT-Image-2.5 System scoring 72.8 and demonstrating early-stage visual state prediction capabilities on real-world tasks; (b) WorldCast reveals substantial gaps between models: even Nano Banana Pro reaches only 42.8 and the best open-source model scores 20.1, with deficits in handling complex context, entangled references, and reasoning-heavy tasks; (c) strong generative models effectively draw on the capabilities of their underlying language models. These findings highlight the need for multimodal generative models that are capable of dynamic planning and reasoning while also being deeply unified to faithfully simulate real-world states.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Orbia: Do Generated Videos Form a Consistent 3D World?
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Video generators serve as interactive worlds for exploration and simulation, yet realistic and visually appealing frames do not necessarily depict a consistent 3D world. Existing benchmarks assess selected geometric properties or use vision-language models to judge memory and consistency, leaving systematic 3D evaluation underexplored. We introduce Orbia, the first benchmark dedicated to a systematic and comprehensive evaluation of 3D consistency in interactive world models. Through controlled exploration and revisit, we organize the evaluation into three dimensions: input preservation, generated-content persistence, and 3D self-consistency. For input preservation, registered RGB-D references and annotated anchors support appearance, geometry, and spatial stability measurements. For generated-content persistence, we compare revisits to regions absent from the input image with their first generated observations to test whether models preserve what they create. For 3D self-consistency, cross-view depth and feature correspondence, regional scale agreement, and held-out Gaussian rendering test whether generated views describe the same 3D scene. Minute-long exploration and revisits further test long-term consistency. Our construction and annotation pipeline brings together public datasets, self-captured scenes, and simulation, yielding 720 instances across indoor and outdoor environments and six exploration-and-revisit protocols. Evaluation spans 27 text-, action-, and camera-conditioned models through native-interface adapters. Our Orbia benchmark provides a systematic basis for diagnosing 3D inconsistency and developing more persistent video world models.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Technical Report; 70 pages, 43 figures, 12 tables; Project page at https://orbia-bench.github.io/ Code at https://github.com/worldbench/Orbia Dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Orbia/Orbia

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Learning Not To Interfere: Adapting Experts For Model Merging
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Model merging has shown that multitask models can be created by directly combining the parameters of different models that are each specialized on tasks of interest. However, models trained independently on distinct tasks often exhibit interference that degrades the merged model's performance. To solve this problem, we formally define the notion of Cross-Task Interference as the drift in the representation of the merged model relative to its constituent models. Reducing cross-task interference is key to improving merging performance. To address this issue, we propose our method, Resolving Interference (RI), a light-weight adaptation framework which disentangles expert models to be functionally orthogonal to the space of other tasks, thereby reducing cross-task interference. RI does this whilst using only unlabeled auxiliary data as input (i.e., no task-data is needed), allowing it to be applied in data-scarce scenarios. RI consistently improves the performance of state-of-the-art merging methods by up to 3.8% and generalization to unseen domains by up to 2.3%. We also find RI to be robust to the source of auxiliary input while being significantly less sensitive to tuning of merging hyperparameters. Our codebase is available at: https://github.com/pramesh39/resolving_interference

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: PhyMix: Towards Physically Consistent Single-Image 3D Indoor Scene Generation with Implicit--Explicit Optimization
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Existing methods for single-image 3D indoor scene generation often produce visually plausible results that violate real-world physical constraints, limiting their reliability in robotics, embodied AI, and virtual environment design. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Physics Evaluator that assesses four aspects (geometric priors, contact, stability, and deployability) through nine sub-constraints, establishing a benchmark for evaluating physical consistency. Our analysis reveals that even state-of-the-art methods produce scenes with substantial physical inconsistencies despite their visual plausibility. To address these limitations, we propose a framework that incorporates feedback from the Physics Evaluator into both training and inference to improve the physical plausibility of generated scenes. Specifically, PhyMix comprises two components: (i) implicit alignment via Scene-GRPO, a critic-free group-relative preference optimization strategy that uses physical evaluations to guide the generator toward physically plausible layouts, and (ii) explicit refinement via verifier-guided agentic repair, which translates evaluator diagnostics into executable scene-editing skills to correct residual violations at inference time. PhyMix unifies physical evaluation, preference-based alignment, and agentic inference-time correction to improve physical plausibility while retaining the observed scene content. Experiments show improvements in reconstruction quality and physical plausibility, while qualitative examples on stylized and real-world images illustrate the applicability of the framework beyond synthetic inputs.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Naka-GS: Naka-Guided Chroma Correction and Point-Prior Compaction for Low-Light 3D Gaussian Splatting
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Low-light inputs obscure scene content, distort color, and corrupt geometric priors, substantially degrading 3D Gaussian Splatting. Although image enhancement can recover visibility, it often introduces chromatic deviations and fine-scale artifacts that propagate through multi-view reconstruction. Moreover, dense point priors can further amplify these errors and increase optimization cost. To address the coupled challenges, we present Naka-GS, a low-light 3DGS framework that jointly improves observations and Gaussian initialization while retaining the standard 3DGS renderer and training objective. Our Naka-Guided Chroma Correction treats a fixed bionic response as a photometric anchor and learns bounded, frequency-decoupled luminance and chromatic corrections, preserving fine structures while suppressing residual color and boundary artifacts. The corrected views are reconstructed into dense scene priors, which a lightweight, non-learned Point-Prior Compaction Module refines through voxel pooling and distance-adaptive progressive pruning. On eight scene-disjoint RealX3D scenes, Naka-GS achieves 20.735~dB PSNR, 0.7408 SSIM, and 0.3340 LPIPS. PPM reduces initialization from 1.00M to 59.52K points and shortens average 3DGS optimization time by 37.7%.The code is available at https://github.com/RunyuZhu/Naka-GS

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Moment-Video: Diagnosing Temporal Fidelity of Video MLLMs on Momentary Visual Events
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress in general and long-form video understanding, yet their ability to capture and use brief, answer-critical visual evidence remains underexplored. Momentary actions or state transitions may determine an answer while occupying only a small fraction of the video. Performance on broad video understanding tasks alone does not establish whether models can reliably identify and use this temporally localized evidence. We introduce Moment-Video, a benchmark for evaluating temporal fidelity through momentary visual event understanding. Questions are constructed around visually observable events or event sequences, requiring models to notice, count, describe, or reason about transient evidence. The benchmark contains 1,000 human-verified video-QA pairs across seven domains and 25 subcategories, covering four tasks: Temporal Occurrence, Temporal Counting, Action Description, and Temporal Reasoning. We evaluate 34 proprietary and open-source MLLMs. Under the main evaluation settings, the best-performing model, Seed-2.0-Pro, achieves 39.6% overall accuracy, while most open-source models remain below 25%. Diagnostic analyses show that denser frame sampling improves some models, but substantial errors persist even when sampled frames cover all annotated necessary event intervals in an audited subset. Performance also declines on longer videos, suggesting additional temporal-localization challenges. By exposing these limitations, Moment-Video provides a diagnostic benchmark to guide the evaluation and development of video MLLMs that more reliably understand brief, answer-critical visual events.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: InkSight: Offline-to-Online Handwriting Conversion by Teaching Vision-Language Models to Read and Write
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Digital note-taking is gaining popularity, offering a durable, editable, and easily indexable way of storing notes in a vectorized form, known as digital ink. However, a substantial gap remains between this way of note-taking and traditional pen-and-paper note-taking, a practice that is still favored by a vast majority. Our work InkSight, aims to bridge the gap by empowering physical note-takers to effortlessly convert their work (offline handwriting) to digital ink (online handwriting), a process we refer to as derendering. Prior research on the topic has focused on the geometric properties of images, resulting in limited generalization beyond their training domains. Our approach combines reading and writing priors, allowing training a model in the absence of large amounts of paired samples, which are difficult to obtain. To our knowledge, this is the first work that effectively derenders handwritten text in arbitrary photos with diverse visual characteristics and backgrounds. Furthermore, it generalizes beyond its training domain into simple sketches. Our human evaluation reveals that 87% of the samples produced by our model on the challenging HierText dataset are considered as a valid tracing of the input image and 67% look like a pen trajectory traced by a human.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Accepted by Transactions on Machine Learning Research

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Learning Topology-Aware Representations for Mechanics-Relevant TPMS Metamaterials
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Learning informative representations of mechanical Triply Periodic Minimal Surface (TPMS) metamaterials is important for mechanics analysis and structural design, yet existing methods have rarely explicitly supervised learned representations with information about global structural connectivity that is relevant to mechanical response. We propose a topology-aware representation learning framework that integrates persistent homology into a DMAE backbone to explicitly encode global structural connectivity. A persistence-guided masking strategy prioritizes patches associated with persistent topological features, while an auxiliary persistent-homology decoder encourages the latent representation to retain information about topological feature counts across connected components, tunnels, and voids. We evaluate the learned representations on two complementary TPMS datasets using family classification, mechanical-property classification, unsupervised clustering, and regression. Across the two datasets, our method demonstrates strong performance in both structural family and mechanical-property classification, improving family classification by up to 3.9% while achieving the best linear-probe performance. More notably, unsupervised property-clustering performance improves by up to 26.7% and 51.5% across the two datasets, while strong regression performance is retained with $R^2=0.993$. These results establish persistent topology as an effective inductive bias for representation learning of complex three-dimensional mechanical metamaterials.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Morphology-aware deep learning predicts colorectal cancer survival from whole-slide images
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary:
Background: Five-year survival prediction from hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide images could support risk stratification, but the task is weakly supervised, and the tissue morphologies carrying prognostic information remain incompletely characterized.
  Methods: We conducted a retrospective secondary analysis using TCGA-COAD/READ (n=562) for morphology-specific analysis, Alliance/ CALGB 89803 (n=424) for model development, and SurGen (n=218) for external evaluation. We propose MorphContrast, a morphology-aware contrastive multiple-instance learning framework that uses tissue labels as structural supervision for five-year survival prediction. MorphContrast combines gated-attention pooling with three auxiliary objectives: patch-level morphology labels define within-patient contrasts, outcome concordance or discordance defines cross-patient contrasts within matched morphologies, and diversity regularization discourages representational collapse. Morphology-matched patches from patients with discordant outcomes serve as hard negatives, encouraging prognostic discrimination within comparable histologic contexts.
  Results: Morphology-specific models show weak but distributed prognostic discrimination: adipose tissue achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.622, stroma achieves 0.604, and both perform comparably to tumor epithelium (0.601-0.605). On Alliance/CALGB 89803, the single model achieves an AUC of 0.642, while the post hoc ensemble reaches a pooled out-of-fold AUC of 0.70 and a risk-group hazard ratio of 3.79 (95% confidence interval: 2.55-5.63). On the external SurGen colon cancer cohort (n=218), the single model and ensemble achieve AUCs of 0.669 and 0.678, respectively.
  Conclusions: These findings support tissue morphology as structural supervision for outcome-aware representation learning in colorectal cancer prognosis.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Supplementary material included: one figure and two tables

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: NeuroDETR: Multiscale Discrete Spatiotemporal Tokenization for Asynchronous EEG Event Detection
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Asynchronous EEG event detection supports practical brain-computer interfaces by identifying event classes and temporal boundaries directly from continuous recordings without predefined event boundaries at inference time. The primary challenge lies in extracting event-related patterns embedded in ongoing background activity. To address this, we propose \textbf{NeuroDETR}, a discrete spatiotemporal multiscale framework that combines structured tokenization with event-aware feature refinement. Multiscale temporal codebooks capture brief responses and sustained dynamics, while Spatial-Pyramid VQ hierarchically encodes spatial structure across EEG channels. These complementary representations form a compact event memory for jointly classifying events and estimating their onsets and offsets. Before tokenization, we apply FOCAL, an event-aware sparse attention module that uses predicted event presence to guide temporal feature refinement and spatial aggregation, emphasizing likely event periods while preserving context across the recording. Experiments on eight EEG datasets that span diverse paradigms demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. These findings provide a basis for the development of BCI systems that recognize meaningful neural activity during continuous interaction and monitoring.

Information Retrieval.title: Creating SquashFS Images to Support HPC and AI Datasets
Information Retrieval.summary: HPC users often download datasets on HPC systems for analysis and processing. When these datasets are comprised of hundreds of thousands (or more) of small files, accessing them in parallel can put a tremendous burden on the metadata servers of central parallel file systems. If the dataset is read-only, an effective solution is to compress the dataset into a SquashFS image. There are, however, a number of workflows that can be used to create such a dataset image, and we observed that some were more efficient than others. To provide more effective guidance for our userbase, we benchmarked eleven different workflows for creating SquashFS dataset image files of datasets with thousands to millions of very small files. We took into account whether the data arrived as tar.gz, zip, or files-and-directories downloads, whether the image creation was on the central file system or local compute node storage, and the number of SquashFS file compression threads used. This paper shares the results of these benchmarks and provides recommendations to HPC system users toward the best workflows to use for SquashFS image creation.
Information Retrieval.comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, IEEE High Performance Extreme Computing (HPEC) Conference 2026

Information Retrieval.title: From Clicks to Intent: Cross-Platform Session Embeddings with LLM-Distilled Taxonomy for Financial Services Recommendations
Information Retrieval.summary: Sequential user behavior modeling is widely adopted in industrial recommender systems; however, significant gaps remain in financial services, where pre-login web interactions and authenticated in-app experiences differ drastically. Specifically, pre-login web users typically explore new products, whereas logged-in app users focus on account servicing. Due to the challenge of cross-channel entity resolution (e.g., matching anonymous web sessions to authenticated mobile accounts), web-based intent signals remain underutilized for post-authentication personalization. Existing methods for capturing web-based intent are often ad-hoc and narrow, lacking the flexibility to support both quantitative downstream recommendations and qualitative understanding at scale. In this work, we propose a scalable and dual-purpose intent prediction framework for web-based interactions and demonstrate its applicability for personalization. Our approach transforms raw web clickstreams into two outputs: a self-supervised Transformer encodes multi-modal clickstreams into a compact session embedding, while an LLM-based taxonomy generation and distillation pipeline produces interpretable intent labels. Our system demonstrates that self-supervised clickstream representations combined with LLM-distilled taxonomies can jointly serve quantitative tasks and qualitative understanding in production: on the mobile homepage tile ranking task, the session embedding improves macro Recall@1 by 1.88% and reduces Log Loss by 13.38% over production baselines. On the user conversion prediction task, the embedding outperforms the LLM labels by 4.3% on micro F1, while the distillation layer delivers interpretable labels at ultra-low latency with only a 7% performance drop.
Information Retrieval.comment: Dianjing Fan and Yao Li equally contributed to this work. 7 pages, 1 figure

Information Retrieval.title: UniRec: Bridging the Expressive Gap between Generative and Discriminative Recommendation via Chain-of-Attribute
Information Retrieval.summary: Generative Recommendation (GR) reframes retrieval and ranking as autoregressive decoding over Semantic IDs (SIDs), unifying the multi-stage pipeline into a single model. Yet a fundamental expressive gap persists: discriminative models score items with direct feature access enabling explicit user-item crossing, whereas GR decodes over compact SID tokens without item-side signal. We formalize this via Bayes' theorem: ranking by p(y|f,u) is equivalent to ranking by p(f|y,u), which factorizes autoregressively over item features, showing that a generative model with full feature access matches its discriminative counterpart, with any practical gap stemming solely from incomplete feature coverage. We propose UniRec with Chain-of-Attribute (CoA) as its core mechanism. CoA prefixes each SID sequence with structured attribute tokens:category, seller, brand, before decoding the SID, recovering the item-side feature crossing that discriminative models exploit. Since items sharing identical attributes cluster in adjacent SID regions, attribute conditioning yields a measurable per-step entropy reduction H(s_k|s<k,a) < H(s_k|s<k), narrowing the search space and stabilizing beam search. We further address two deployment challenges: Capacity-constrained SID introduces exposure-weighted capacity penalties into residual quantization to suppress token collapse and the Matthew effect; Conditional Decoding Context (CDC) combines Task-Conditioned BOS with hash-based Content Summaries to inject scenario signals at each decoding step. A joint RFT and DPO framework aligns the model with business objectives beyond distribution matching. Experiments show UniRec outperforms the strongest baseline by +22.6% HR@50 overall and +15.5% on high-value orders. Deployed on Shopee's e-commerce platform, online A/B tests confirm significant gains in PVCTR (+5.37%), orders (+4.76%), and GMV (+5.60%).

Information Retrieval.title: GenState-AI: State-Aware Dataset for Text-to-Video Retrieval on AI-Generated Videos
Information Retrieval.summary: Existing text-to-video retrieval benchmarks often permit matching from static appearance, making it difficult to determine whether models capture state changes and final outcomes. We introduce GenState-AI, a benchmark comprising 956 AI-generated videos and 195 verified state-change queries across Toy, Cartoon, Home, and Manipulation domains. Its construction uses prompt-controlled variants that target either conflicting temporal/state outcomes or semantic substitutions. Following human verification, all valid videos contribute to subset-level retrieval pools, while complete query-specific triplets support diagnostic hard-negative ordering. We evaluate VCF-Lik, Qwen3-VL, and LanguageBind using both standard Recall@K and triplet-based consistency metrics. Qwen3-VL (8B) achieves the best macro-average R@1 and triplet consistency, while LanguageBind obtains the highest semantic discrimination accuracy. However, stronger retrieval does not consistently yield correct hard-negative ordering, and Qwen3-VL and LanguageBind remain weak on Manipulation triplets, where VCF-Lik performs substantially better. GenState-AI therefore provides a controlled diagnostic testbed for distinguishing global retrieval quality from fine-grained temporal and semantic grounding in AI-generated videos.

Information Retrieval.title: QASP: Query-Adaptive Robust Vector Search Policy
Information Retrieval.summary: A fundamental challenge of vector search is achieving consistently high recall while minimizing computational costs. Fixed search parameters cause significant performance variance across queries, and conventional evaluation on average recall masks these per-query disparities. We introduce QASP (Query-Adaptive robust vector Search Policy), which predicts the complete recall progression curve per query via a single upfront supervised regression, from which a search policy is derived for any recall target; this avoids iterative model invocations during search or separate predictors per target. By predicting normalized recall values with scale-invariant features and pre-search inference, QASP generalizes across recall targets, index configurations, and datasets. The fine-grained progress predictions further enable a lightweight reactive complement that adjusts search depth based on predicted-versus-observed deviations without additional inference. We prove that QASP requires a finite training sample independent of dataset size and dimensionality, that it matches or improves on the best fixed-policy loss up to a vanishing statistical error, and that its data access savings over fixed probing grow exponentially in intrinsic dimensionality. Experimentally, QASP achieves significantly lower recall variance and deviation from target, higher query satisfaction rate, and scales to large data and hierarchical indices without retraining, achieving 99% recall with 80% less data access. Our implementation can be found at https://github.com/amazon-science/QASP.

Information Retrieval.title: Data Curation and Model Souping: Unlocking Qwen3-0.6B for MS MARCO Passage Ranking
Information Retrieval.summary: This report studies passage retrieval and re-ranking on the MS MARCO benchmark using lightweight Qwen3-0.6B models. Across three experimental settings --- BM25-then-reranking task, corpus-wide dense retrieval task, and dense retrieval then re-ranking task --- the results demonstrate that competitive ranking performance can be achieved without complex architectural modifications, custom loss functions, or cross-encoder distillation. Instead, substantial gains stem from data-centric strategies: corpus-targeted continued pre-training, rigorous data curation, hard-negative mining, training--inference distribution alignment, and weight merging via Model Soup. In particular, Model Soup delivers marked performance gains while preserving the inference efficiency of a single model. These findings highlight how data curation and weight merging can push sub-billion-parameter models to state-of-the-art performance. My models can be downloaded from Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/shuguangh/models

Information Retrieval.title: CASI: Credit Assignment via Set Intervention for Agentic Retrieval
Information Retrieval.summary: Large language models increasingly generate multiple retrieval actions jointly, while downstream systems often provide only one reward for the resulting set. Broadcasting this reward provides a valid score-function gradient estimator for the expected set-level objective, but does not determine a coalition-dependent within-set attribution. We introduce CASI (Credit Assignment via Set Intervention for Agentic Retrieval), which constructs the missing counterfactual information through snapshot-grounded set intervention: generate and retrieve once, hold replayable snapshot components fixed, and evaluate alternative subsets under common conditions. Shapley aggregation converts these marginals into within-set credit, which bounded zero-sum advantage shaping incorporates into policy optimization. For m >= 4, singleton, leave-one-out, and full-set endpoints do not generally determine the Shapley allocation; under additive set values, extra coalition evaluations are redundant. In a five-action sponsored-search setting, exhaustive auction replay over 1,200 requests reveals substantial coalition dependence. Under the training-time evaluator, CASI achieves the highest median cosine similarity to a replay-defined Shapley reference among evaluated credit rules; under a sensitivity backend, CASI does not outperform Singleton. Across five independent training runs, CASI-trained policies achieve higher held-out auction-replay set value than Singleton- or Broadcast-trained policies. In a randomized seven-day production A/B test on 10% of traffic, the CASI-trained policy yields an observed 3.51% lift in the primary advertiser-value metric over production control.

Information Retrieval.title: HEM-Med: A Hierarchical Agentic Memory Framework for Safe Multi-Center Medication Recommendation
Information Retrieval.summary: Medication recommendation (MR) is critical for clinical decision support. While existing MR methods are mostly designed for single-center learning, where only one independent hospital is involved, multi-center MR with hospitals of different scales has become increasingly demanding in practice. In multi center settings, abundant data from large medical centers can improve recommendation performance for low-resource centers. Despite a few preliminary attempts on this task, two critical gaps remain. Gap 1: Existing multi-center methods fail to disentangle transferable cross-hospital clinical experience from hospital-specific prescribing patterns, limiting clinical feasibility and physician acceptance. Gap 2: They commonly overlook multi label safety constraints of MR, including drug-drug interaction risks and local formulary feasibility, which are essential for safe real-world deployment. To address these gaps, we propose HEM-Med, a novel hierarchical agentic memory framework for multi-center MR. To address Gap 1, we design a disentangled hierarchical memory module that builds patient-level medication context attribution records and disentangles them into cross hospital experience memory and hospital-specific residual memory. To address Gap 2, we introduce a safety-aware medication set generation module, which integrates dual-level experience retrieval with safety-aware set decoding to produce clinically relevant, safer, and locally adaptive medication recommendations. Experiments on a real-world multi-center eICU dataset show that HEM-Med outperforms representative transfer learning, LLM-based, and MR baselines in terms of both recommendation accuracy and safety.

Information Retrieval.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation to Support Railways Engineering Tasks: A Case Study
Information Retrieval.summary: The growing number and complexity of technical regulations represent an important challenge for all professionals in regulated industries. This paper describes a case study, from design to deployment, of building a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system for the consultation of complex technical regulations in the railway domain. Although developed for the railway sector, this testimony of an industrial experience is of particular value for technical domains where regulatory compliance and accurate information retrieval from complex documentation are essential requirements. It also constitutes a human-centered approach for implementing LLM-powered technical documentation consultation across various regulated industries, balancing technological capabilities with domain expertise.

Information Retrieval.title: Relevance Supervision Can Teach Neural Retrievers to Prefer LLM-Generated Text
Information Retrieval.summary: Recent studies show that neural retrievers often exhibit source bias, ranking LLM-generated passages above semantically similar human-written ones, which threatens the reliability of modern information access systems. While this bias is often viewed as a model-level property, we show that relevance supervision itself can induce it. Empirically, source bias is clearest in relevance-supervised retrievers, and the same encoders become more LLM-preferring after relevance fine-tuning. We trace this effect to surface-level artifacts in supervised retrieval data: annotated positives and negatives differ systematically in properties such as fluency and lexical specificity, and these differences parallel those between LLM-generated and human-written passages. As a result, retrievers can learn artifact-based shortcuts for relevance. We further show theoretically that, under contrastive learning, artifacts that reliably separate positives from negatives can be encoded into learned relevance scores. Motivated by this mechanism, we propose complementary strategies that reduce source bias during training and at inference: balancing artifact distributions in negative sampling and removing the artifact-aligned embedding component, respectively. Overall, our findings support a data-centric view of source bias: retrievers may prefer LLM-generated text not merely because of inherent model properties, but because relevance supervision teaches them to rely on surface-level artifacts.

Information Retrieval.title: XViewRank: Overlap-Conditioned Score Fusion for LLM-Augmented Sparse Retrieval
Information Retrieval.summary: Large language models can reduce vocabulary mismatch in sparse retrieval by generating alternative views of a query. Once these views are searched independently, however, their ranked lists may be complementary, redundant, or affected by query drift, making fixed fusion suboptimal. We present XViewRank, a lightweight retrieval-side method for conditionally fusing BM25 results from an original query, a hypothesis view, and a step-back view. For each pooled candidate, XViewRank retains three normalized BM25 scores and three query-level overlaps between the retrieved result sets. A small nonlinear scorer uses the overlaps as context that changes how the view-specific scores are interpreted, without jointly encoding query and passage text. Under a matched-input protocol, XViewRank improves nDCG@10 and MAP numerically over reciprocal rank fusion on both TREC DL 2019 and 2020, with a statistically significant MAP gain on DL19. Additional analyses show that the clearest benefit occurs when the view rankings have low agreement, while the evidence on DL20 is weaker. The results support overlap-conditioned score fusion as a compact retrieval-side alternative to fixed fusion, while also delimiting where its advantage is empirically established.

Information Retrieval.title: Reading the Neighborhood: Text-Attentive Graph Reranking for Automated Subject Indexing
Information Retrieval.summary: Subject indexing assigns descriptors from a controlled vocabulary to bibliographic records, a task characterized by thousands of labels, few positive examples per label, and a long tail of rarely used descriptors. Existing extreme multi-label classifiers treat the vocabulary as a flat list, ignoring the semantic relations that thesauri encode. We present TAGHN, a heterogeneous graph reranker over a per-document subgraph of retrieved candidates augmented with the thesaurus neighborhood. The relevance of a candidate descriptor is estimated jointly from its similarity with the document and also the degree to which the candidate's thesaurus neighborhood matches the document content. A decomposed scoring head combines interpretable graph-derived features with retrieval signals. On STW, an economic thesaurus of 6,198 descriptors, TAGHN reaches 0.380 macro F1 against 0.346 for a fine-tuned cross-encoder and 0.278 for a fixed-vocabulary XMLC classifier. In terms of micro F1, it outperforms reranking models and stays competitive (-3.0) with the best fixed-vocabulary XMLC model. Qualitative analysis shows the graph resolving errors that per-label scoring cannot, selecting a narrower gold descriptor where an unstructured reranker settles for its broader parent.
Information Retrieval.comment: Presented at the ACM/IEEE-CS Joint Conference on Digital Libraries (JCDL) 2026

Information Retrieval.title: When RAG Doesn't Help: LLMs for Plausible Material Prediction of Vehicle Components
Information Retrieval.summary: In this work, we explore whether LLMs can predict and explain plausible materials for vehicle components such as brake discs or fuel injectors without extensive fine-tuning. We compare a standard generative LLM baseline, single-pass Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and an iterative Chain-of-Verification (CoVe) variant across two LLMs, using a domain-filtered Wikipedia corpus that proved helpful in prior work. As no gold standard exists, we develop and release a reusable web-based annotation tool supporting crucial functions for structured domain-expert judgments, such as highlighting, ratings and ranking. Expert agreement is reasonable for plausibility, lower for ratings. LLM-based generation compares favorably to prior work. RAG and CoVe do not improve on it and are partly rated worse by experts. Contrary to prior work, Wikipedia-based retrieval does not help in our setup.

Information Retrieval.title: EviRerank: Adaptive Evidence Construction for Long-Document LLM Reranking
Information Retrieval.summary: Decoder-only LLM rerankers struggle with long documents: inference is costly and relevance signals can be diluted by irrelevant context. Motivated by an attention analysis indicating a consistent degradation trend when non-relevant text is appended, we propose EviRerank, an evidence-based long-document reranking framework for decoder-only LLMs. EviRerank (i) scores document blocks with a lightweight selector (BM25, bi-encoder, or cross-encoder), (ii) constructs a compact reranking context under a hard token cap by dynamically budgeting evidence blocks with Adaptive Evidence Budgeting (AEB) and adding a global summary cue via Summary Augmentation (SA), and (iii) reranks with a decoder-only LLM. Across TREC DL'19, DL'22, DL'23, and MLDR-zh, EviRerank consistently outperforms full-document LLM reranking and strong block-selection baselines while substantially reducing the required input length. On TREC DL'19, EviRerank reaches up to 0.744 nDCG@10 while substantially reducing reranking latency. Additional RankZephyr-7B experiments confirm transfer to listwise reranking under matched context budgets.

Information Retrieval.title: Ground-Truth Subgraphs for Better Training and Evaluation of Knowledge Graph Augmented LLMs
Information Retrieval.summary: Retrieval of information from graph-structured knowledge bases represents a promising direction for improving the factuality of LLMs. While various solutions have been proposed, a comparison of methods is difficult due to the lack of challenging QA datasets with ground-truth targets for graph retrieval. We present SynthKGQA, an LLM-powered framework for generating high-quality Knowledge Graph Question Answering datasets from any Knowledge Graph, providing the full set of ground-truth facts in the KG to reason over questions. To demonstrate its utility, we apply SynthKGQA to ogbl-wikikg2, a Wikidata-derived KG, and validate generated items against an up-to-date dump of Wikidata to create GTSQA. This new dataset is specifically designed to test zero-shot generalization with respect to unseen graph structures and relation types, enabling us to analyze the abilities and limitations of SOTA graph retrieval approaches at an unprecedented level of granularity. We also show that KG retrievers trained on GTSQA can transfer to a human-curated benchmark, and that the ground-truth subgraphs produced by SynthKGQA provide a better training supervision signal than previously-used heuristics.
Information Retrieval.comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)

Information Retrieval.title: Self-Retrospection Distillation: Turning Post-hoc Experiences into Prior Foresight
Information Retrieval.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) turns agent experience into learning signals primarily through scalar outcome rewards after interaction. For group-relative objectives, however, this signal vanishes when all rollouts receive the same reward, even though their trajectories may reveal useful information about what the task requires and how the agent fails. We ask a complementary question: can hindsight teach an agent what it could have anticipated before acting? We introduce prospective learning, which uses post-hoc experience to supervise foresight predictions from the pre-interaction view, and instantiate it with Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD). Intuitively, a completed trajectory reveals knowledge that would have been useful and pitfalls that should be avoided; SRD distills this privileged hindsight into trajectory-blind foresight of the same policy. Foresight serves only as a training target and need not be explicitly generated at inference time. Across 10 tool-integrated reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks, SRD complements RLVR and self-distillation baselines with gains of up to 24.2 pp. Its advantage is especially pronounced when reward contrast is scarce: when 37--98% of rollout groups are reward-uniform across model scales, yet SRD can still exploit learning signal from sampled trajectories. In the 2B setting, where 98% of groups are all-failure, the RLVR training ends up at 0.0% success, while adding SRD reaches 60.6% under the same rollout budget. Our results suggest that post-hoc agent experience is useful not only for evaluating or improving behavior, but also for shaping predictive representations before available interaction. Training code can be found at https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/SRD.

Information Retrieval.title: Computed, not Memorized: Bit-Factorized Identifiers for Efficient Generative Retrieval
Information Retrieval.summary: Generative retrieval is known for its efficient end-to-end indexing and retrieval. In particular, numeric Document Identifiers (DocIDs) are generally more efficient because they are shorter and generally fixed-length sequences over a small vocabulary, requiring fewer decoding steps during beam search. However, they tend to generalize poorly to unseen documents and must be learned during indexing-stage training. In this paper, we propose a numeric DocID design for generative retrieval that enables better adaptation to unseen documents without retraining. Our DocID design inherits the language model's knowledge: each DocID is a sequence of tokens factorized into bits, and each token is scored as the sum of its bits. Unlike existing numeric DocIDs, whose tokens carry meaning only through embeddings memorized during indexing training, each bit here derives its meaning from the model's representation. Therefore, the DocIDs of unseen documents remain scorable without retraining. Experiments on three benchmarks show that our DocID design substantially improves unseen-document retrieval while maintaining comparable performance on seen documents. It achieves over 20 percentage points higher Hit@10 on unseen documents and up to 7 times lower inference latency than existing numeric DocID designs on NQ320K and TriviaQA, while performing only 3 percentage points below weight-update methods on MS MARCO without additional training. These results show that an appropriate DocID design can heavily reduce retraining costs when adapting generative retrievers to new documents.

Information Retrieval.title: Gauge-Invariant, Parameter-Insensitive Regularization for Potential Recovery from Flow on Directed Graphs
Information Retrieval.summary: Recovering a latent potential from observed flow on a directed graph (a discrete Poisson problem with Dirichlet boundaries) is ill-posed, and the standard fix backfires: ridge regularization shrinks toward a gauge-meaningless origin, collapsing and reversing the recovered ordering ($+0.81\to-0.42$ rank correlation against a planted ground truth). The gauge-invariant graph Dirichlet energy removes the hazard and delivers parameter-insensitivity: the estimate is stable across four orders of magnitude in $λ$, whereas ridge inverts the ordering for every $λ>0$. We prove the reduced solve is SPD and preserves dynamic range exactly where ridge collapses it, and localize absorbing boundaries from flow alone via a Poisson residual. The $H^1$ seminorm is classical; what is new is the gauge diagnosis, the parameter-insensitivity it buys, and an ablation showing the result is robust to the extraction method. On three public clickstream corpora the gauge-invariant estimate retains $28$--$41\%$ of the interior dynamic range while ridge collapses to as little as $0.2\%$. The same gauge invariance carries into graph neural networks -- neutralizing the constant mode per layer prevents the oversmoothing that collapses a deep directed GCN -- linking this classical inverse problem to a central question in graph learning.
Information Retrieval.comment: 19 pages, 6 figures, Proceedings of the Fifth Learning on Graphs Conference (LoG 2026), PMLR 338

Information Retrieval.title: ARAFA: An LLM-Generated Arabic Fact-Checking Dataset
Information Retrieval.summary: Automatic fact-checking poses a significant challenge in Arabic natural language processing due to the scarcity of datasets and resources. In this manuscript, we introduce Arafa, a new large-scale dataset for fact-checking in Modern Standard Arabic, constructed through an automated framework leveraging large language models (LLMs). The dataset was constructed through a three-step pipeline: (1) claim generation from Arabic Wikipedia pages with supporting textual evidence, (2) claim mutation to generate challenging counterfactual claims with refuting evidence, and (3) an automatic validation step to validate that the generated claims are either supported or refuted by their accompanying evidence, or if the evidence does not provide enough information to judge the validity of the claims. The resulting dataset comprises 181,976 claim-evidence pairs labeled as supported, refuted, or not enough information. Human evaluation carried out on a test sample from the dataset demonstrated strong inter-annotator agreement (kappa = 0.89) using Cohen's Kappa for supported claims and (kappa = 0.94) for refuted claims. Automatic validation based on a human-evaluated sample achieved 86% accuracy for supported claims and 88% for refuted ones. To showcase Arafa's value as a resource for automatic Arabic fact-checking, four open-source transformer-based models were fine-tuned using Arafa, with the top-performing model achieving a Macro F1-score of 77% on the test data. In addition to Arafa being the first large-scale dataset for Arabic fact-checking, our framework presents a scalable approach for developing similar resources for other low-resource languages.

Information Retrieval.title: On the Impact of Graph Neural Networks in Recommender Systems: A Topological Perspective
Information Retrieval.summary: In recommender systems, user-item interactions can be modeled as a bipartite graph, where user and item nodes are connected by undirected edges. This graph-based view has motivated the rapid adoption of graph neural networks (GNNs), which often outperform collaborative filtering (CF) methods such as latent factor models, deep neural networks, and generative strategies. Yet, despite their empirical success, the reasons why GNNs offer systematic advantages over other CF approaches remain only partially understood. This monograph advances a topology-centered perspective on GNN-based recommendation. We argue that a comprehensive understanding of these models' performance should consider the structural properties of user-item graphs and their interaction with GNN architectural design. To support this view, we introduce a formal taxonomy that distills common modeling patterns across eleven representative GNN-based recommendation approaches and consolidates them into a unified conceptual pipeline. We further formalize thirteen classical and topological characteristics of recommendation datasets and reinterpret them through the lens of graph machine learning. Using these definitions, we analyze the considered GNN-based recommender architectures to assess how and to what extent they encode such properties. Building on this analysis, we derive an explanatory framework that links measurable dataset characteristics to model behavior and performance. Taken together, this monograph re-frames GNN-based recommendation through its topological underpinnings and outlines open theoretical, data-centric, and evaluation challenges for the next generation of topology-aware recommender systems.
Information Retrieval.comment: Accepted for publication in Foundations and Trends in Information Retrieval

Information Retrieval.title: The Dice Roll Method: A Standardized Protocol for Repeated-Query Auditing of Large Language Model Brand Recommendations
Information Retrieval.summary: Background: Researchers increasingly use repeated identical prompts to audit stochastic variation in large language model (LLM) brand recommendations, yet no standardized protocol exists for setting iteration counts, selecting stability metrics, or establishing reliability thresholds. Objective: We formalize the Dice Roll Method as a reusable protocol for repeated-query auditing of LLM brand recommendations, grounded in a generative model of temperature-scaled nucleus sampling. Methods: Total response variance is decomposed into sampling, prompt-phrasing, run-to-run, and model-version components. The stack: a negative-binomial mixed model with iterations as repeated measures; Cliff's delta as the distribution-free effect size; dependence-preserving bootstrap; simulation-based power; a generalizability-theory decomposition; drift diagnostics on pinned snapshots. We reanalyse five brand-recommendation auditing studies: approximately 190,000 observations, 270+ brands, 6 languages, iteration counts 5 to 40. Results: The recomputed D-study supports no fixed tiers. Across 250 distinct questions (S5), G is 0.96 at five runs and 1 to 2 runs reach 0.80, also within each model. For five versions of one question (S1 Valentine's subset, Gemini) it is 0.27 (95% CI 0.00 to 0.52), which fixes no run count. Runs follow from a pilot: n = 4 x residual / cell variance. Simulated single-cell power for a large Cliff's delta is 0.15 to 0.19 at five runs and 0.8 at 15 to 25. The four metric families (count, set, embedding, PASOR) are complementary. A pre-registered external validation on three independent corpora reproduces the D-study prediction in 37 of 39 cells with no failures; fixed tiers do not transfer. Conclusion: The protocol gives repeated-query auditing of LLM brand recommendations a statistically principled footing under the conditional, non-Gaussian structure of real autoregressive generation.

Recomputed from the study data. Section 6 results are unchanged. Supersedes Research Square rs-8980233 and rs-9496731 (v1 named rs-8883056 in error)
